#5808. Senate advances federal energy permitting bill

The Senate is fast tracking legislation that would reduce permitting times for energy projects, but possibly to the detriment of longstanding policies protecting the environment.

The Associated Press reported that the Senate voted 73-25 to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). The bill was drafted in response to growing electricity costs from sources like grid-connected hyperscale data centers. By reducing permitting times, energy projects, like solar energy or onshore oil drilling, could address rising energy costs.

However, environmental groups consider BAAJA a reckless response to an immediate need for more power. The bill would amend sections of the Natural Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act of 1973 to shorten review periods for new projects, and reduce which projects actually require reviews under these acts.

“We shouldn’t and don’t need to endanger our wildlife just to save a few dollars on gas. We shouldn’t and don’t need to weaken the rules that protect our water from pollution in order to build more clean energy. We shouldn’t facilitate more global-warming air pollution. And we definitely shouldn’t be taking away the public’s right to weigh in on projects that can ruin their environment, make them sick and lessen their quality of life,” said Lisa Frank, executive director of Environment America.

Despite the bill’s threat to environmental measures, the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) has voiced its support for BAAJA, as have hundreds of companies in the solar and energy storage industry. More than 300 groups co-signed a letter addressed to Congress yesterday imploring the House pass this bill.

“Americans urgently need lower energy costs, a better electric grid and more nergy made in the U.S.A. This bipartisan legislation delivers all three,” said Tim Pawlenty, CEO of SEIA.

SEIA conducted an analysis that claims passing BAAJA could spur 167 GW of new solar energy on the grid between 2028 and 2035, while curbing the country’s CO2 emissions by 20%.

“Updating and expediting transmission and clean energy permitting is essential to delivering lower costs, reduced air, water and climate pollution, protecting communities and expanding the grid for the American people,” said Loren Blackford, executive director of Sierra Club, in a press statement on Sunday. “But rushing legislation that erodes Tribal sovereignty and people’s right to have a say in what is built in their communities, abandons clean water safeguards and wildlife protections, while further enabling a rogue president that is waging a war on clean energy and our public lands is not an acceptable outcome.”

Billy Ludt is managing editor of Solar Power World and currently covers topics on mounting, inverters, installation and operations.

#5807. Bigger than Godzilla!

Fortescue’s plans for the Pilbara include wind turbine blades that are bigger than Godzilla.

While Fortescue’s boss hobnobs with King Charles III and chats about sustainability, under the Commonwealth Nature Initiative, progress continues towards real zero in the remote Pilbara of Western Australia. See the video of Andrew and Charles here.

As part of Dr Andrew Forrest’s vision of real zero by 2030, Fortescue is installing wind turbines with a blade length of 89 metres. Bigger than Godzilla! Have we got your attention now? The blades will be deployed at the Nullagine Wind Farm in the Pilbara region of Western Australia. They will arrive by ship at the Port Headland project site. Fortescue has done major upgrades to allow the blades easy access and to minimise impact on local traffic. The community will also receive regular updates throughout the delivery program to keep residents informed.

For global readers, I would like to point out that Fortescue’s mining operations and land tenements in the Pilbara region of Western Australia cover more than 87,000 square kilometres (34,000 square miles). This is roughly the size of Austria (83,879 km²), Ireland (84,421 km²), or Serbia (88,361 km²), and more than twice the size of countries like the Netherlands (41,850 km²) or Switzerland (41,285 km²). And for USA readers, Fortescue’s land holdings alone are larger than South Carolina, West Virginia, or Maryland, and roughly the same size as the entire state of Maine or Indiana. But only one eighth the size of Texas.

You will have read about Twiggy Forrest’s achievements and vision of real zero mining operations here and here. Fortescue is taking steps to educate the public on decarbonisation. You need to take the people with you, especially the shareholders. Here is a great video produced by Fortescue to show how to decode decarbonisation. The Godzilla-sized wind turbines are part of an ecosystem. They will provide the power to recharge the electric dump trucks. But just how do you recharge a 240 ton dump truck in a timely manner? Using 6MW robotic fast charging, of course, thus eliminating 26% of Fortescue’s emissions — and saving a dump truck of money in the process.

CleanTechnica reported on the acquisition of Williams Racing 5 years ago, in order for Fortescue to access Williams’ fast-charging technology. It has taken some time, but it looks like everything is coming together. I still have the picture in my head, inspired by this acquisition, of huge dump trucks doing F1 races in the red dust of the Australian Outback. Beyond the fantasies of Mad Max, even. While we are indulging in mental gymnastics, the Fortescue video tells us that 6MW of charging is like boiling 1,875 electric kettles all at once. That’s a lot of tea or coffee! A less than 30-minute charge will give 4 hours of operation for the truck. The charging equipment has to be resilient, as the Pilbara is hot and dusty, with temperatures in summer over 40 degrees and down to below freezing on winter nights.

Episode 2 answers the question “Can a green grid power a mining operation 24/7?” It’s a big ask. Fortescue is the fourth largest iron ore producer in the world, exporting 200 million tons a year. The advantages: Fortescue achieves cost savings, does good for the climate, and keeps control of its energy. In the current global situation, I would add energy security.

The Pilbara has 300 days a year of irradiation and Fortescue plans to harvest that with a planned 1.5 gigawatts of solar farms. Eventually, this will be backed up with 900 MW wind and balanced by 5 GWh of battery storage — enough electricity to power 800,000 homes on solar alone. This is all connected by a high-voltage green grid consisting of 600 km of transmission lines. “A city scale power system in the middle of nowhere.” The green operation does not draw from the public grid; not the distant future, but right now.

Fortescue is not just content to reduce emissions for its mining operations; it is also working on green steel — a product for the future. Fortescue reports that it has produced its first hot metal via an electric smelting process in a pilot project at Christmas Creek. Initially using a blended feedstock, as the commissioning process continues, it is expected to be able to handle Pilbara iron ore. Larger scale production is the aim. At the moment, the focus is on testing, refining, and optimising the process.

Fortescue Metals Chief Executive Officer Dino Otranto said: “This is a significant milestone for our Green Metal Project and another step towards producing commercial-scale green metal in Australia.

“For decades Australia has exported iron ore to the world. The next opportunity is to create more value from that ore by producing green metal here at home.

“The real opportunity goes beyond green metal. It’s about building a new industrial economy around Australia’s renewable energy advantage.

“Nobody has solved green metal production using Pilbara ore at commercial scale yet. That’s the challenge we’re taking on.”

I’m looking forward to more good news of progress towards real zero from Fortescue Metals. Have CleanTechnica readers noticed any other mining companies heading down the same path? If so, make a comment below. Even in the “hard to decarbonise” mining sector, electricity sourced from renewables and stored in batteries is the way to go for cost saving, climate protection, and keeping control of energy inputs. In Australia’s Pilbara, the future is bright and electric.

#5806. FDA Slaps New Safety Warning on GLP-1 Drugs

— Required labeling will warn of potential risk of NAION, a potentially blinding eye condition

The FDA is requiring manufacturers of all GLP-1 drugs to update their prescribing information to include a warning about the potential risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION), a rare but potentially blinding eye condition.

Cases of NAION have been documented across all currently marketed GLP-1 products, according to the agency.

Healthcare providers should "instruct patients to immediately report sudden onset of acute, painless, decreased vision; visual field deficits; or other visual disturbances in one eye," the FDA stated in a safety communication on Monday. "If NAION is suspected, promptly refer the patient to an ophthalmologist for evaluation. Consider discontinuing the GLP-1 [receptor agonist] in patients who develop NAION, unless the benefits of treatment clearly outweigh the risk."

NAION occurs when blood flow to the optic disc is reduced. Beyond the painless vision loss -- often noticed upon waking -- symptoms can include blurred or missing visual fields, color distortion, and reduced central visual acuity. Its exact triggering mechanism remains poorly understood and animal data on GLP-1 drugs did not further elucidate a potential mechanism for the higher risk observed with the drugs, the FDA said.

The agency's action follows a wave of studies suggesting a potential link between GLP-1 drugs and NAION, including a 2024 study in JAMA Ophthalmology involving semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) that FDA said prompted its review. Europe's drug regulator warned about the risk 17 months ago.

In a meta-analysis of randomized trials performed by the FDA, the agency identified 15 probable NAION events among more than 134,000 patients. Of those, 10 cases occurred among the roughly 78,000 treated with GLP-1 drugs, none were in those randomized to other glucose-lowering medications, and five occurred in placebo recipients. Incidence was 6.4 cases per 100,000 person-years among the GLP-1 drug recipients compared with 3.8 cases per 100,000 person-years among patients receiving a non-GLP-1 medication or placebo.

A retrospective cohort study performed by the FDA involving type 2 diabetes patients showed no significantly increased risk for NAION with GLP-1 agonists versus SGLT2 inhibitors (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.91-1.54) but an increased risk was seen compared with DPP-4 inhibitors (HR 1.43, 95% CI 1.02-2.01).

Common risk factors for NAION include smoking, diabetes, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea, anemia, and chronic kidney disease. Patients with a history of NAION carry an increased risk for recurrence.

Patients and clinicians can report suspected adverse reactions associated with GLP-1 medications to the FDA's MedWatch reporting program.

#5805. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Cheated On His Marriage With An Alleged Spy

Happy Monday! It's November 9, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift — your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition we're looking at Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair, and rough times over at Tesla and SpaceX. We'll also look at dealerships sharing your most sensitive conversations with AI, and Toyota trying to get a break on tariffs.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO and leather jacket enthusiast, cheated on his wife. This is a simple fact, admitted by Huang. The part of the situation that's still up for debate is whether the woman Huang cheated with is a Chinese spy sent to gather intel on Nvidia's precious advanced micro devices. If so, it could spell trouble — not just for Nvidia, not just for autonomous vehicles, but for everything wrapped up in the AI bubble. From Bloomberg:

Nvidia Corp.'s investigation into Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy raises a series of once-unthinkable questions, including whether the man at the center of the AI boom is at risk of losing his job.

Nvidia shares slid about 5% in premarket trading after Huang disclosed the romantic relationship in a memo to employees, a decline that would mean a roughly $225 billion loss in market capitalization. The company's board is assembling a committee of independent directors who will work with outside counsel to investigate the matter.

With the stunning revelation, investors need to consider a range of possibilities that could affect not just Huang and Nvidia, but the entire artificial intelligence industry. Nvidia, the leading maker of AI chips, has used its financial strength to back dozens of major players, from frontier labs like OpenAI to cloud computing players like CoreWeave Inc. Huang has also been among the most forceful advocates for the benefits of AI, from Washington to Wall Street.

If there's one thing that rich guys love more than acting incredibly divorced, it's cheating on their spouses in order to get divorced in the first place. There's a possible trajectory here where Jensen Huang's inability to keep it in his pants crashes the global economy — the AI bubble, its circular financing, and everything invested in it all comes tumbling down.

Tesla and SpaceX have been teasing a merger for a while now, bringing CEO Elon Musk's biggest companies — Tesla, SpaceX, Twitter, xAI — under one cult of personality stock ticker. Shares have been climbing in anticipation of such a merger, but the midterm blue wave likely took that off the table. Now, investors are balking. From Reuters:

Nov 5 (Reuters) – Shares of Elon Musk's companies ‌SpaceX and Tesla slumped on Thursday, extending losses from the previous session, as investors worried that Democratic wins in the US midterm elections could slow data center build-outs.

SpaceX, which has leaned into the ​AI data center boom, is headquartered in Texas alongside Tesla, where Democrats won ​the races for Senate, governor and attorney general on Tuesday. Musk ⁠had spent heavily to back Republicans in the midterms.

The selloff also reflects worries that ​Democratic gains could bring tougher scrutiny of Musk's businesses.

Tesla has recovered some since this Reuters piece — it's up a bit over 5% today as of this writing — but it's still down from pre-midterm highs. SpaceX is on a near-identical trajectory, but slightly higher. Don't worry, Elon still has money.

Are you concerned that AI might not be invading enough of your private life? Well, now you can rest easy with the knowledge that dealerships are bringing it in — not just on the sales floor, but in the F&I box. Some dealers are recording those conversations, and running them through AI in order to upsell you more effectively. From Automotive News:

Until this year, Len Stoler Automotive Group's finance offices generally sold one product per vehicle.

Now, that number is closer to two. The group says employees — coached in part by artificial intelligence — deserve some of the credit.

Len Stoler Automotive uses AI-powered software to record sales interactions with customers. Part training tool and part compliance coach, the technology provides feedback to the group's sales teams to help them highlight the value of a product, rather than push a customer to buy more.

Auto News frames this as a positive, a way for dealers to make more money, while to me it's horrifying. Yeah, why not share all my most private financial information with an AI in real time — an AI with the explicit intent of upselling me on stuff I don't need? Even if it doesn't work, which is likely, that AI now has my financial data to lose in some data breach down the line. Cut it out, dealers.

#5804. The Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 Red Cross Edition — CleanTechnica Tested

Jackery was one of the earliest portable power station producers to bring these beautiful creations into the mainstream. They have a line of portable power stations and proprietary portable, foldable solar panels that continues to make them one of the top go-to options for anyone looking for power on the go.

Recently, they launched a Red Cross Edition of their popular HomePower 2000 Plus v2 that donates a portion of the profits to the Red Cross to support first responders. We covered these limited edition units when they first hit our radar during our visit to Jackery’s headquarters in Shenzhen, China, and now they are finally moving into production.

Jackery donates 10% of profits from this series to donate portable power stations to rescue organizations and emergency response teams, supporting disaster relief and recovery efforts. At the volumes Jackery is producing, that’s a meaningful step in the right direction to putting portable power stations into the hands of the first responders who need them most.

Disclaimer: Jackery provided the Red Cross edition of the 2000 Pro V2 portable power station to the author for the purposes of this review.

Charging up the unit is a simple matter thanks to its ability to pull a charge from multiple sources. Right out of the gate, you can charge from a normal 120V AC wall outlet at around 1,600 watts. This is typically the maximum you can safely charge from any wall outlet without overheating cables or outlets, and the Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus V2 makes full use of it. In our testing, we pulled 1,590W from the wall for a full charge from empty in an hour and a half.

You can also charge up the unit with solar panels, which with 800 watts of solar can recharge the battery from fully drained to overflowing in 3.2 hours. Jackery uses a proprietary solar connector, so keep that in mind before you buy your battery and/or panels.

You can also charge it up via your car’s 12V automotive outlet (requires optional car charging adapter for $29.90), which can push power out at about 100 watts. This varies slightly from car to car, but the fact of the matter is that you’re generally limited based on the factory wiring for what that outlet can handle.

Jackery knew about that, so they developed their own DC-to-DC charger for combustion vehicles. This optional accessory costs $239, but taps into the full power of your alternator and can pull up to 600 watts. This is a faster charge and can top up the battery in about 4 hours, but requires a bit of extra planning and work and assumes you’re running a combustion vehicle. It’s worth consulting with a professional if you’re going to go this route, as alternator wiring and max output varies greatly from car to car.

Electric vehicles typically don’t have a 12V outlet, opting for USB-C instead. Unfortunately, the Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus V2 Red Cross Edition is not able to charge up via USB-C at any power level. Fortunately, many electric cars come with integrated AC outlets, which can be used to charge the battery up in a pinch.

I tested this in my Cybertruck and achieved similar charging rates to what I was able to achieve at home, which tops the battery up in about an hour and a half. This is a great option to use while fast charging on a road trip because you can charge for about 30 minutes at a time to keep your portable power station charged up without having to run the inverter while driving, which drains the battery faster.

When it’s time to tap into all that stored power, the Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus v2 Red Cross Edition is ready. It can push out 2,400 watts of continuous power with surge capability of up to 4,800W. Given that this is a compact 2 kWh unit weighing just 21 lb, that’s a pretty solid level of power output that it can handle. Power output has continuously been improving with each successive generation and Jackery continues to be near the top of the pack with its numbers.

It’s obviously up to the task of powering lightweight items like drones, laptops, portable lights, charging radios, keeping the internet on, and even powering your fridge in an emergency. On the home front, it’s also a great option. Thanks to its LFP chemistry, Jackery expects you to get 6,000 charging cycles out of this battery, which equates to more than 16 years of daily cycling.

Even though it is such a compact unit, it should be able to keep essentials running at home — including your refrigerator, freezer, computer, lights, smartphone, Wi-Fi, etc. — for nearly 10 hours. That should get you through most outages, and, honestly, if you’re having longer outages than that, you probably want to look into a home battery system. Or you can tap into the HomePower 2000 Plus v2 Red Cross Edition’s ace up its sleeve….

The Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus V2 Red Cross edition can actually add more capacity. It has a special port on the left side of the unit that lets you plug in any of Jackery’s Battery Plus expansion batteries for up to 12kWh of total capacity. That’s a 6× increase over this unit’s installed capacity and lets you scale your storage capacity as you find new use cases for it.

The use case for this at home is really keeping the lights and and the refrigerator running during an emergency and using solar or a generator to charge up when it runs low. It can absorb up to 800 watts of solar from an attached array, meaning you can fully charge it in about an hour and a half depending on the sunlight you’re getting. Even in terrible conditions, it’s still going to charge up in just a couple of hours.

We put this beast to use running a portable refrigerator, lights, USB, charging our laptop and phones, and even charging a few portable batteries for us to take with us hiking. This unit kept our devices charged up for several days of fun in the desert. It was great knowing that after we were done charging our devices, the battery would top itself up again from the attached solar panels.

No matter how many devices we plugged in, including our usual kitchen torture test, its 2,400W of power output was more than enough to keep everything running. The surge power is pretty cool too because it allows the unit to absorb the spikes in consumption that come from a lot of devices when you first turn them on.

But we wanted more. So we pulled out some new winter heaters and really made the Jackery sweat. Each of these heating units can pull up to 1,500 watts each, which is about the max you can get from a standard 15A outlet. We plugged both into the Jackery and cranked them up to the max. I’m personally thrilled to have more energy-hungry appliances to torture — I mean test — portable power stations with.

Playing with all of their settings, we had them pulling almost 3,100 watts constantly before the Jackery finally decided to throw in the towel. It kept them running for several minutes over its own 2,400 watt constant power output rating, which was impressive, especially considering how compact this thing is.

It’s exciting to see Jackery continuing to push into new battery technologies, but in this case, this is the same battery they sell as a normal unit, just rebranded to highlight the great work being done at the Red Cross and to give some of the profits back in the form of product.

That’s worth celebrating, and it’s exciting to see Jackery leading the charge to enable first responders with technology without charging governments or consumers more money for the same product.

Or maybe you just like a bright red unit that’ll make it hard to lose or forget. Whether you’re heading out on a camping trip or heading back to the house after a long week out in nature, the bright red colorway of this unit is sure to stand out.

For more information about the Jackery HomePower 2000 Plus Red Cross Edition or to purchase one for yourself, head over to Jackery’s official website.

#5803. These Are The Worst Road Trips You've Ever Taken

Not every road trip is an adventure that you'll remember for the rest of your life. We wish every day on the road could be sunshine and rainbows, but sometimes your vacation is just nonstop thunderstorms. God forbid you decide January is a good time to visit a national park, but the highway to get there is unplowed and has turned into a stranded-car sanctuary.

We asked our readers last week about the worst road trip they've ever taken. I honestly couldn't conceive how bad things could get when stuck inside a car with other people for hours on end. Commenters submitted some truly absurd anecdotes, ranging from being locked inside a scorching, aluminum-topped pickup bed with his brother as kids to someone's beloved Border Collie defecating in his girlfriend's lap. I love driving, but have road trips been a secret form of torture all along? Without further ado, here are the long-distance drives you'd love to forget:

Right around the turn of the century, my wife and I had to pick up our stepdaughter at Chicago Midway Airport so she could come home after spending Christmas with her bio-dad.

Nothing majorly bad happened to us, but it was a very white-knuckle drive.

A huge blizzard hit in the morning when we were supposed to leave. Bio-dad said her flight still hadn't been canceled, so we set off on our way (early, of course).

What normally would have been a 2-hour trip turned into a 4-hour one. Literally, when we got off the highway at our exit to go to Midway, he calls and says her flight was canceled.

So we turned around and headed back home. That was a 6-hour trip going about 30 MPH the whole way. That was the worst because I was really tired by then. It was dark by that point, so you really couldn't see anything but the snow coming down. My mind kept seeing cars spin out in front of me, when they weren't.

We made it almost all the way home but got stuck in the middle of the road about 3 miles from home. A nice couple was there in a 4X4 when it happened, so they gave us a push and that got us home.

We did get stuck in the driveway, but that was something to deal with the next day.

I never want to drive 10+ hours in a blizzard ever again!

In the days of paper maps, was skiing with my girlfriend in Vermont, and we planned to drive to a town about 10 miles away for a nice dinner (jacket and tie, candlelight, etc.). Driving along, some roads plowed, some not, but no biggie. Start driving up a hill, encouraged by the fact that, although there was snow on the road, there were tracks, and I had 4WD. As the snow started getting deeper, my brain clicked: those are snowmobile tracks. Stopped the car, did a 34-point turn to make sure I stayed on the road and didn't go into a ditch or a gully, and coasted back down the hill. Ended up grabbing pizza right near the place we were staying.

Around 2017, driving my wife's new-to-us BMW with runflats to Blacksburg, VA from CT. Car was CPO and had bout 20K miles. We hit a mega hole on I-78 in NJ near the PA line. Two passenger-side tires blew. Torrential rain, 5 a.m. could not see a thing. Pulled over and found a BMW dealer 20 miles away in PA that would open in a couple of hours. Went there and waited. The service manager was great, he looked the car over and told us that the remaining tires were new and that changing just two was not a problem. Three months later, the front diff fails. $6700 estimate, a small battle with BMW corporate, but once we produced the service doc with the dealer's recommendation of only two tires they fixed the car under the warranty. Thing is, they did a repair, not a replace and sure enough the thing fails again just out of warranty. Traded it in for an Accord. A word of caution: NEVER buy an AWD, especially German, if you don't know the tire replacement history. Essentially, tires need to be replaced in fours unless the others are very fresh. My trusted indy tells me that as little as 9mm can make the difference!!!!

We drove from Charleston, SC to the Outer Banks of NC in August in a 1989 Jeep Wrangler with no AC in the rain. The windshield kept fogging up and the road conditions were awful. We had to make time to meet the ferry schedule and it was sweaty, back pain-filled, bouncy 9 hours...

Amarillo to Dallas for Christmas break in school. My Mazda3 hatch was loaded to the gills with everything we needed to bring home during the break, plus our snowboard gear. A small spot was carved out for our Border Collie to sit. Unbeknownst to me, my girlfriend (now wife) had fed him 6 egg yolks from her egg white omelet that morning and had given him terrible gas. We stopped often to get him to poop, but nothing. Then, in the final 5 miles to her parents' home, he panicked in the backseat. We were on an under-construction part of highway with no exits in sight and no shoulder when he jumped from the back seat into the front seat (he is now properly secured while in the car). I'm trying my best not to crash while looking for an exit while she grabs him and bear hugs him to herself. I then hear her say, "he's sh*tting, he's sh*tting," as she holds him tight and has diarrhea all into her lap. I pull into a Taco Bueno parking lot and she takes him out. I go in and get cleaning supplies and we clean him up, throw away her snuggy-like robe, and put him in a trash bag with his head sticking out for the 10-minute drive to her parents' house. The only casualty was the passenger seat belt, which she accidentally let fully retract and required a full deep clean/disassemble and a 48-hr air out.

Houston to Chicago and back in a brand new BEV. Having spent 15 years in PHEVs, expected refueling to be a minor issue. It was a major issue; chargers were often inaccessible, broken, vandalized, few and far between. Yes, one can spend a tremendous amount of time gaming out a plan for slightly better results, but lotza time and only slightly better results. The stalling out of the plans to make electric cars viable, by the Republicans, cost manufacturers TONS of money and great frustration for me personally.

"Of all the sad words of tongue or pen, the saddest of these: it might have been." (if not for the lingering orange fart in the White House)

May 2019. 7 friends, 4 guys and 3 girls on a 2-week road trip from New Orleans to Yosemite and back. At least that was the plan. Our last hurrah trip before graduating college didn't go right from the start. Imagine 7 adults in a rented Escalade PLUS 2 weeks' worth of gear! We overpacked from the start. We had to leave all our tents behind except for one, which was my friend's dad's old Boy Scout tent that smelled like toe cheese and had old wax coating peeling off. We left late because of the packing, so we were constantly behind schedule as a result. We also overplanned things to do so this meant we'd see something for 5 minutes and then have to keep driving so we wouldn't miss something else! Texas went on forever. The big crater in Arizona? Didn't get to see it, had to drive right by. The Grand Canyon? We got there late in the day instead of the morning, so instead of hiking and seeing it we got to look at it for 30 minutes, 15 of which were obscured by clouds. Then we got sleeted on and had to leave. Vegas? Giant waste of time where we all secretly confessed to looking at flights home and tried to salvage the trip... and friendships. Drove through Death Valley in the middle of the night. Tensions were high. Some people were controlling. There were tons of fights and crying. It was too cold to camp so we diverted to San Diego for a few days which saved us. Then Santa Fe. Then 20 hours through storms in Texas and then home. Too many people and too much time. Never again.

The past two summers, I've taken my 1979 El Camino from northern Wisconsin to be a part of Elcofest in Indiana the final weekend in July with no A/C. Both times it was 95ºF, muggy, and rainy, so we had to keep the windows up. For me, those were among the best road trips I've ever taken. But if you ask the wife, she'd probably say they were among the worst.

In the late '70s, I drove from Saint Paul up to northern Minnesota in -10 degrees to go cross-country skiing. Unfortunately, the heat in my rusted-out VW Squareback was not up for the trip. My passenger rode in a down sleeping bag. We had to constantly scrape the ice off the inside of the windows and windshield. My passenger refused to ride back with me, instead opting for the bus from Bemidji.

Ah, Yes. The old air-cooled VW winter experience, all bundled up with one gloved hand on the wheel, and the other with an ice scraper!

Indiana to John Pennecamp State Park in the Florida Keys. In summer. My brother and I rode in the bed of my dad's truck (a single-cab F-100) under a beercan-thin aluminum topper for ALL the miles. Occasionally one of us would be allowed to go through the rear sliding window and sit in the cab with mom and dad. We could open the windows to the topper, but then it got REALLY loud, so we had to use that sparingly. We mostly just baked.

Bonus points: we were sitting on a plywood platform covered in that 1970s green outdoor grass carpet, and under the platform were several scuba tanks which we had been told were full and super dangerous and could explode. Because 1970s parents thought that sort of thing was hilarious.

It was hot, loud, uncomfortable and we spent the whole time going down afraid for our lives. It was years later that our parents explained that the tanks were empty; they just wanted us not to move around too much.

#5802. Ford Drops Hint About New Fathom EV Battery Life

The Ford Motor Company has been playing its forthcoming Fathom electric pickup truck close to the vest, releasing few details ahead of volume production except for the MSRP of $28,350. Still, some clues have dropped. The latest news involves a newly released real-life data analysis of five-year battery capacity for the Ford Mustang Mach-E. The findings raise expectations for the next generation of Ford EVs, namely, the Fathom, which is the first vehicle to roll down the tree-like assembly line of the company’s new “Universal EV” platform.

On one level, the comparison between the Mach-E and the Fathom EV battery is apples-to-oranges. The 2021 Mach-E deployed [correction: NCM (nickel-cobalt-manganese) batteries with Standard Range at 68 kWh usable capacity as launched, and Extended Range at 88 kWh usable capacity as launched]. Ford is equipping the Fathom with an LFP (lithium-iron-phosphate) EV battery. LFP is a relatively new, more economical formula than Li-ion. All else being equal the tradeoff is lower range, though some Ford watchers point out that drivers can order their Fathom with an optional extended-range battery.

The point is that the 2021 Mach-E is old news. The new news is the forthcoming Fathom, which Ford has been regularly teasing as the first product of its secret, not-so-secret “skunkworks” team for the past five years or so. The addition of a cost-cutting, internal inverter for bidirectional charging is the topic of the most recent news drop, indicating that Ford expects Fathom drivers to use their EV battery for stationary applications as well as drive time.

Drivers who routinely use the bidirectional feature will likely put their Fathom through more charging cycles than a typical EV, and prospective buyers will need some assurance that their zero emission pickup will be up to the task.

And, that’s where the 2021 Mach-E data comes in. Ford has just released the 5-year numbers for retained battery capacity over time, and they look pretty good. By releasing the data now, when the Fathom is nearing volume production, Ford has raised expectations that the new electric pickup truck will deliver similar, if not better, longevity.

Correction: The Mach-E data doesn’t just look pretty good, it looks very good. Ford deployed its telematics platform to assess more than 36,000 Mustang Mach E’s in the “class of 2021,” driven in the US and Canada over an average ownership period of 5.2 years as of August 2026, during which time drivers clocked a collective 2 billion miles.

The 2021 Mach-E was sold with both standard and extended range battery packs, and the data combines both variations.

Relative to the Fathom’s bidirectional charging feature, the key finding is that high-mileage vehicles scored well. “More than 2,000 owners have crossed 100,000 miles on their original battery pack while maintaining >91% average health,” Ford explains. In the 2021 cohort, 30 drivers also ran past 200,000 miles while retaining an average capacity of about 88%.

Ford, which graciously shared an embargoed press statement with CleanTechnica over the weekend, also emphasizes that 95% of the 2021 Mach-E’s landed between 87% and 97% health, indicating that a relatively small number of outliers brought the average down to 92% overall.

The Mach-E data will surprise nobody who has been paying attention to the latest news about EV battery lifespan. As it turns out, EV batteries last far longer than first anticipated. That’s significant enough when an EV battery is deployed for mobility purposes. Capacity retention takes on extra importance when the same battery is used to manage electricity use in homes and other buildings.

Ford provided some insights last month, when it posted a long form article describing the Fathom’s built-in inverter. An inverter is a device that converts the DC current from an EV battery into the AC current used in homes. A typical bidirectional charging system requires the property owner to install a wall-mounted inverter, adding another layer of expense. Ford has absorbed the cost of the inverter into the Fathom itself, a decision aimed at encouraging drivers to make use of bidirectional charging at home. The company has also been working with utilities to help motivate drivers to take advantage of the feature.

With bidirectional charging, EVs realize their full potential as rolling, zero emission power generating stations. Drivers can use bidirectional charging on an emergency basis, to keep the lights on at home in case of a grid power outage. They can also take advantage of utility incentives, which reward EV owners for deploying their stored ectricity during periods of peak demand or other stresses on the grid, benefiting all ratepayers in the service territory.

Some US utilities already offer discounted or even free rates for EV owners who charge up their battery during off-peak hours. Try that with your gasmobile!

Stay tuned to this channel for further details about the Fathom and its battery. In the meantime, some Ford dealers have been passing along information from the automaker’s HQ. Here’s a representative example from the DC-area dealer Koons Ford:

“Battery options beyond the standard-range configuration have not been announced yet. Ford has confirmed a long-range battery option is planned and that its upcharge will be significantly lower than what Lightning buyers experienced, but specific range figures and pricing tiers are not yet public. This page will be updated as Ford confirms additional specifications.”

Okay, so much for that. Tonkin Hillsboro Ford in Oregon is hardly more forthcoming:

“Ford Fathom pre-orders will begin in early 2027, with a starting MSRP of $28,350 for the standard-range battery. While some specifications are still to come, there’s already plenty to know about this new Ford electric truck.”

“Ford has not yet released projected EPA-estimated driving range figures for the Fathom,” Tonkin elaborates. “The vehicle is currently being introduced with a standard-range battery, but an official EPA range estimate isn’t available yet.”

“This is one area where shoppers will need to wait for additional information,” the dealer adds.

Hmmm…let’s turn to the automotive press, where EV Charging Stations was somewhat more forthcoming. “The 2027 Ford Fathom electric pickup truck will not exceed 300 miles of range in its base form, but it likely will with the optional larger battery,” EVCS reports.

“The Ford Fathom has a 400-volt LFP battery system and 48-volt auxiliary electrical architecture. The truck features a cell-to-pack battery system (no modules), with prismatic battery cells being structural elements of the vehicle,” EVCS elaborates, further speculating that the extended-range battery could involve a higher-performing LFP formula or a switchover to the familiar NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt) concoction.

EVCS also calculates that the standard EV battery will yield a range of under 220 miles, with the extended range version coming in at 300 miles, as Ford has indicated.

Meanwhile, the Detroit Free Press has noticed that a fully loaded Fathom with all the bells and whistles still comes in around the $40,000 mark, well below the $54,000 average cost of new EVs.

We won’t have long to wait for the full details to come out. Last week, Torque News was among those reporting that the Fathom is well into the final validation stages leading to full volume production.

With sales expected to begin late next year, the Fathom will face some competition from other EV makers that are aiming at the electric pickup truck market. One pickup stakeholder that Ford won’t have to worry about, though is Tesla, which is planning to halt production of the Cybertruck next year.

#5801. Was Superglue to Blame for His Lung Nodule?

— Benign nodule discovered during CT scan for abdominal pain

A CT scan turned up an incidental nodule in the lung of a patient being evaluated for kidney stones, and clinicians' best guess is that it had something to do with superglue.

The patient, a man in his 40s, presented to an emergency department in Belgium with severe abdominal pain, and a CT scan revealed kidney stones, Pauline Vermoesen, MD, of Ghent University in Belgium, wrote in BMJ Case Reports.

However, there was also an incidental finding of an air-filled pulmonary nodule, about 16 mm in diameter, they wrote. They followed the patient via CT scan for about 9 years.

The nodule turned out to be a pneumatocele, a gas-filled, thin-walled cavity more commonly seen in children, and typically found in the context of infection, trauma, or hydrocarbon aspiration. In this case, the patient did report that a few weeks before turning up at the ED with abdominal pain, he had "accidentally inhaled superglue."

"In the absence of infection or trauma, glue aspiration is considered the most likely cause, although without histopathological confirmation a definitive causal relationship cannot be established with certainty," Vermoesen and colleagues wrote.

The patient was a non-smoker, with no history of a respiratory infection or thoracic trauma. The nodule hadn't been there on a CT scan done 7 years prior to the kidney stone finding, the authors noted.

Positron emission tomography-CT scanning showed minimal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake, suggesting it was a benign lesion. Serial CT imaging over a total of 9 years showed, "progression from a solid nodule to a thin-walled cystic lesion consistent with a pneumatocele," they wrote.

The pathophysiology of pneumatocele likely involves parenchymal necrosis and a check-valve mechanism, Vermoesen and colleagues wrote, whereby partial bronchiolar obstruction leads to air trapping and distal cystic dilatation.

This rare case in an adult demonstrates the benign and uncomplicated evolution of a pneumatocele. In most cases, pneumatoceles regress and resolve spontaneously, they wrote.

"In our patient, however, the lesion persisted throughout the 9-year observation period, a pattern also observed in a case series of two pneumatoceles arising during sorafenib therapy, which likewise failed to fully resolve during follow-up," they wrote.

The aspirated glue was identified as a neoprene-based contact adhesive containing hydrocarbon solvents.

Serial imaging allowed differentiation from other cystic lung lesions such as bullae, blebs, or true cysts, "enabling us to forgo invasive diagnostic work-up and supporting the conservative management approach adopted in this patient, given the absence of complications," the authors concluded.

#5799. EVs Displace 5 Times More Oil Globally Than They Did 5 Years Ago — Analysis

Five years on from Glasgow, EVs have proved the single most effective way to curb oil use, says T&E.

At COP26 in Glasgow, twenty-four countries and a group of leading car manufacturers committed to ending the era of fossil-fuel powered vehicles by 2040 “or earlier”. Five years and two energy crises later, oil savings from EVs globally are up fivefold, new T&E analysis shows. EVs are the single most effective way of cutting oil demand, improving energy security and reducing emissions, says T&E.

While battery electric vehicles (BEVs) represent just 4.2% of the global fleet, they now account for 25% of all new car sales worldwide – up from 6.6% five years ago. This surge has pushed oil displacement from 215,000 barrels a day in 2021 to 1.2 million barrels a day today, or roughly 1.2% of global consumption.

At the same time, electric buses now make up 5% of the global fleet, battery electric trucks are at 1% but in some countries exceed 50% of new sales. T&E estimates these vehicles avoid as much as 320,000 barrels a day. As road transport burns close to half of all the world’s oil, transitioning to EVs is crucial in reducing oil dependency. As the global car and truck fleet continues to grow, EVs are the only thing stopping runaway oil demand, warns T&E.

As electrification takes center stage at this year’s COP, current policies put battery electric cars on track to displace roughly 5.8 million barrels of oil a day by 2034 — matching the sustained disruption seen during the 2026 crisis. Accelerating EV adoption will be crucial to preventing future oil shocks, according to T&E.

Antony Froggatt, senior director at T&E, said: “Electric vehicles are the single most effective way of cutting oil demand. Right now the only winners in our oil addiction are fossil fuel giants and petrostates. Places with near 100% sales of EVs like Norway, Denmark and Hong Kong have effectively insulated themselves from future shocks. Five years after Glasgow, EVs stand as one of the clearest victories in global climate history. At this year’s COP, world leaders must set binding electrification targets. Not just for the climate, but for national security.”

BEVs on the road now avoid more than 200 Mt of CO2-equivalent a year. According to T&E, rapid transport electrification is a vital part of the wider energy transition by providing essential grid flexibility and storage. Just as past COPs accelerated the global boom in wind and solar, backing for electric vehicles at COP31 can deliver the same breakthrough, slashing oil demand and driving emissions down.

[1] Displaced oil is estimated from daily per vehicle savings: about 0.019 barrels per car (derived from Ember), 0.2 per truck (IEA) and 0.15 per bus (bottom-up from typical fuel use and mileage). The 2026 supply loss has been estimated at 5.8 million barrels a day. We use IEA fleet projections for 2030 and 2035 fleet sizes to calculate the offset year of the BEV car fleet. Results exclude plug-in hybrids, vans and two- and three-wheelers.

For the chart, global capacity and generation for up to 2024 come from the US EIA. For 2025, we used IRENA capacity additions and Ember generation data. Values for 2026 are T&E estimates based on Chinese installation data to September 2026 and generation on IEA mid-year growth forecasts. Global BEV sales from Ember.

Transport & Environment’s (T&E) vision is a zero-emission mobility system that is affordable and has minimal impacts on our health, climate and environment. Created over 30 years ago, we have shaped some of Europe’s most important environmental laws.

Washington, DC — In the continued rush to hold a vote during the lame duck session on the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026”, the senators crafting the bill released a manager’s amendment on Saturday. The Senate has scheduled a procedural vote to begin consideration of the draft legislation tomorrow.

On Friday, Sierra Club issued a statement that it could not support the permitting bill as currently written, outlining fundamental changes that must be made. The manager’s amendment partially addressed these concerns, but major substantive issues remain.

“The Sierra Club appreciates the improvements made by the manager’s amendment, but the draft legislation remains deeply flawed. The Senate must allow an open amendment process for additional changes to be made.

“Updating and expediting transmission and clean energy permitting is essential to delivering lower costs, reduced air, water, and climate pollution, protecting communities, and expanding the grid for the American people. But rushing legislation that erodes Tribal sovereignty and people’s right to have a say in what is built in their communities, abandons clean water safeguards, and wildlife protections, while further enabling a rogue president that is waging a war on clean energy and our public lands is not an acceptable outcome.

“Senate Democrats have been given a mandate to act decisively to deliver relief on energy bills and level the playing field for clean energy. They can and must fight for a better deal. Unless additional dialogue and changes can happen, the Sierra Club cannot support this legislation.”

The Sierra Club is America’s largest and most influential grassroots environmental organization, with millions of members and supporters. On Monday, Brent Crude prices fell below the $95 mark, and at the time of writing, a barrel of Brent can be had for $94.77. West Texas Intermediate, on the other hand, slipped below $90 and is down to $88.21 at the time of writing. And if the WSJ's reporting is accurate, those price drops have come because it's looking less likely that Trump will escalate the war he started without congressional approval now that Democrats control both the House and the Senate:

Oil prices fell sharply Monday, with Brent crude dropping more than 3% to below $95 a barrel after President Trump downplayed the prospect of further U.S. attacks on Iran, even as attacks on Saudi Arabia and fresh incidents involving tankers in the Strait of Hormuz highlighted continuing risks to Middle Eastern oil supplies.

Trump said in an interview with CNN Sunday that further U.S. strikes on Iran were highly unlikely as long as negotiations over Tehran's nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz made progress. His comments followed a sharp decline in oil prices last week as traders assessed the prospects for a diplomatic resolution following the Democratic Party's victory in the U.S. midterm elections.

Saudi Arabia is still dealing with its Houthi problem, and that could always derail a peace deal. Especially since Houthi attacks struck Riyadh, hitting an Aramco administrative building but not killing anyone. Additionally, projectiles hit at least one, if not two ships in the area over the weekend. So there's still more to work on, but these days, we'll take any positive sign we can get.

Of course, while this year's midterm election proved to be the biggest win for Democrats since Watergate, Democrats won't take control of Congress until new members are sworn in next year, and they won't have a chance at the White House until the 2028 election. With both the House and Senate, they'll have the power to check Trump and Republicans, but there are still limits on what they can do while Trump's president. As a result, don't expect a peace deal overnight, even if gas gets cheaper. From the WSJ:

However, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said talks with Washington had made no progress and Tehran was waiting to see whether the U.S. administration would change its position following the elections.

Signs of easing supply tightness are also emerging in the oil market. The spread between the nearest Brent futures contracts has narrowed to around $2.60 a barrel from nearly $4 at the end of last week, while physical crude prices are trading below futures, according to MUFG.

With Vance still involved and Stephen Miller now the chief of staff, the Trump White House hasn't magically transformed into a good-guy factory. Vance also appears to regret starting this stupid, pointless war, with the Guardian reporting that the vice president sent Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's supreme national security council, a letter in an attempt to negotiate a peace deal. We've seen wishful thinking drop oil prices before, so don't assume the traders know anything we don't, but the fact that prices aren't rising is at least encouraging.

Maybe, just maybe, the end to Republicans' latest war in the Middle East could finally be drawing to a close. Trump's reversing course on his plans to flatten the entire country of Iran, Vance is already attempting to distance himself from Trump, and with the American people sending a loud and clear message to the rest of the world, it's possible Republican negotiators will be more willing to make a deal that upsets Netanyahu's party in Israel.

Whether that will happen or not still remains to be seen, especially since Trump tends to change his mind based on who he spoke with last or which man speaking with him has a juicier dumper. Republicans could still sink a peace deal, but at least Trump and Vance sound like they're ready to be done. We won't get a very good deal out of any peace agreement, but that's also what happens when you start a pointless war and lose. It's also no reason to continue fighting. Let's end this war and end it now.

#5796. The Flu Shots Are Here! The Flu Shots Are Here!

Every year, we wait on the arrival of this season's annual flu vaccine, patiently biding our time and explaining to our patients that it's coming, any day now, while the manufacturers finish their processes of selecting the candidate strains, making the vaccine, packaging it up, distributing it, and getting it into our hands at the practice through a complex system of logistics.

Every year, it seems to arrive later and later, and often in shorter supplies, than we would hope.

Many of our patient visits in late summer include specific questions: when is the flu vaccine going to be here, when can I get mine?

We usually tell them we're hoping for September but it might be October, but we've had some even later years for delivery, we're hoping to send out an announcement through the patient portal, so as a patient, please be patient.

Sometimes folks can't wait, they are really anxious to get that protection; the minute their pharmacy announces they have it in stock, they go on in and get it.

We're often deluged with messages: please update my chart to show I got the flu vaccine on September 3, at my workplace. And usually within a few days the statewide registry will catch up and dump this into their vaccine immunization history in our electronic medical record.

There always are lots of patients who don't want a flu vaccine, who've never gotten one and never will. No matter how much we try to address their hesitancy and answer their questions, some have a real reason -- some have fears that have grown from social media or friends and family, and some have had a prior severe reaction or side effect. Guillain-Barré. Optic neuritis. Anaphylaxis.

Try as we might, we never get everybody vaccinated, but I'm incredibly grateful that we do such a good job of getting it to everyone we can before flu season is really barreling down in full force.

When I first started out in practice, I never really bothered getting the flu shot.

While I'd had the flu a few times in my life (once a miserable few days spent in bed feeling like death-warmed over), I always figured it wouldn't be that bad and I've always been healthy and I didn't really need the vaccine.

As I matured into my practice, I became more convinced by the arguments of my colleagues and our infectious disease friends and epidemiologists and public health experts, showing that I was actually putting patients at risk, including during that subclinical phase when I would be carrying and shedding the virus and potentially spreading it to my patients, who could fare far worse with a case of influenza than I might.

Now that I've matured even further (and by "matured" I mean "gotten older"), I suddenly find myself qualifying for the "senior flu shot," a milestone I once looked at as being far off in the distance, now suddenly upon me.

Since we got the flu vaccine in our practice this season, it has been incredibly busy, and I haven't had time to get mine. I keep making excuses: I'm going out to dinner or playing squash tonight, big presentation in the morning, I'll get it later.

Suddenly this week, I realized the deadline for all of us at our institution getting vaccinated was upon us, and it was time to get my jab.

In the old days, one of my partners used to give me the flu shot, and I would give him his, but now we want to make sure it gets accurately registered in the system so that Workforce Health and Safety can close our files, mark us as compliant with our mandatory annual influenza vaccination.

So, I dutifully scheduled an appointment at a local pharmacy, and stopped in to check off that box.

Overall, everything went smoothly. One of the folks working behind the pharmacy counter checked me in after confirming my name and date of birth, and I was the only one waiting so the nurse called me right in.

She went through the same process of confirming my date of birth, asked which arm I wanted it in (my right deltoid, since I'm left-handed), a quick pinch, and I was done.

Think how amazing this is: I'm able to get this done, to protect myself and my patients and my family and my friends and community from what could be a potentially deadly illness.

Science and public health and our amazing healthcare system have so much to offer to keep people healthy, to get them healthy, to prevent and treat and cure.

I know some people will read this and scoff, have their arguments about why vaccines are terrible, say we've all been deluded by some secret cabal of people trying to make money and causing some disease or changing my DNA, but for the most part it would be wonderful if everyone would just believe us, let us do right by providing the best care with the best evidence.

Someone can say no, but we should never deny any group of people, any community, any individual, the opportunity to seek the best healthcare they can get.

I'm hopeful as we've seen the results of the midterm elections last week that opportunities to improve healthcare, to bring calmer and saner voices to the table, will revitalize and transform our healthcare system, have it live up to the potential it holds, and take us down a series of brilliant pathways that will allow us to serve our patients as best we can.

#5795. Nissan Brings The Patrol Name Back To The U.S. After Nearly 60 Years ... Kind Of

In a move that's either pure nostalgia-bait or an appeal to hardcore off-road nerds, Nissan is bringing the Patrol nameplate back to the U.S. for the first time since 1969. No, Nissan's Armada isn't getting a name change. Don't freak out, Armada faithful. Instead, as a celebration for the Patrol's 75th anniversary, Nissan is bringing the name back as a trim level on its full-size SUV brute.

Called the Armada Patrol Pro-4X, the body-on-frame SUV adds all sorts of neat off-road extras while also not being terribly different from the normal Pro-4X it replaces, save for new Patrol badging on the tailgate, center console, door sills and floor mats. That's what it's all about, baby. There are also a handful of optional extras, like some very tough-looking Nismo-branded rock sliders and a roof rack with an incorporated light bar, that are new for 2027. They can be had along with Nismo's existing 18-inch Axis wheels, which are wrapped in  BF Goodrich All-Terrain T/A K03 rubber.

Under the hood, you'll find the same twin-turbocharged 3.5-liter V6 as the cool normal Armada, pumping out 425 horsepower and 516 pound-feet of torque. It's paired to a nine-speed automatic transmission that sends power to all four wheels courtesy of a full-time 4WD system and a locking rear differential. To help keep you out of trouble when you're off-road, the Patrol Pro-4X comes with height-adjustable air suspension, underbody armor, and tow hooks.

If you're the type of person who is a real nasty Nissan nerd, or you just love off-roading, perhaps the 2027 Armada Patrol Pro-4X is for you. If that's the case, you've just got to be ready to fork over $81,265, including $2,275 destination. That's no small chunk of change, but it actually undercuts this car's closest rival, the Toyota Sequoia TRD Pro, by $6,855.

I won't lie to ya, I don't completely understand the decision here for Nissan. I mean, Patrol is hardly an established nameplate in the U.S. It only existed here from 1962 to 1969, and it's been gone for a hell of a long time, so I can't imagine there's a ton of nostalgia behind it. I suppose you could point to an appeal to off-roading nerds as a reason for the name addition or perhaps Nissan is getting ready to switch the Armada's name over to Patrol in the U.S., though I sort of doubt that.

Patrol has been a part of Nissan since 1951, so there's obviously a lot of brand heritage behind it. I'm just not sure there's a lot of brand heritage behind it in the U.S. Better late than never, though, and Patrol Pro-4X does sound a bit cooler than just Pro-4X, so who am I to complain?

#5794. West Yorkshire’s £229 Million Bus Decisions Will Outlast Its Operating Contracts

West Yorkshire has made two substantial commitments to its bus network. On November 2, FirstGroup announced a £109 million agreement with the West Yorkshire Combined Authority covering five depots, associated infrastructure and 330 buses, including 79 battery-electric vehicles. The authority is also spending £120 million on more than 250 new buses through a separate programme. These investments will help establish the region’s new franchised Weaver Network, but many of the assets being acquired will remain in use long after the first operating contracts have ended.

West Yorkshire’s fleet and depot commitments illustrate a problem explored in my 83-page report, The Bus Is Not the System. The accompanying TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines which decisions are becoming expensive to reverse and what authorities should establish before making their next commitments.

The Weaver Network changes the relationship between public transport planning and private bus operations. The Combined Authority will specify services and retain responsibility for passenger revenue under its initial large contracts, while private operators deliver the routes. The region is securing assets that will remain important regardless of which company operates the buses. In principle, that can make future competition easier because bidders do not each have to provide a new depot and fleet.

The challenge is that buses, operating contracts and infrastructure follow different clocks. An operating contract might last five or seven years. Vehicles can work through successive contracts, while depot buildings and electrical connections may remain useful for decades. A change in route patterns, population or employment locations can make an established depot less convenient. A bus can often be reassigned, but a multi-megawatt electricity connection cannot be transferred to another site because the network needs charging capacity elsewhere.

West Yorkshire has arranged a staged transition. The five depot sales have completed, while the buses are scheduled to transfer as new franchises begin operating between May 2027 and October 2028. First Bus will continue delivering existing services under temporary depot leases and will manage electrification at Bradford and Huddersfield, with the authority paying for that work. The arrangements allow services and infrastructure development to proceed while ownership and operating responsibilities change.

Securing strategically important depots is a defensible approach. It reduces dependence on an incumbent operator’s control of scarce infrastructure and can help new companies compete for future contracts. The authority also assumes long-term responsibilities for the assets, including maintenance, future electrical capacity and their suitability for a changing passenger network. A depot can be worth purchasing without every potential alternative having been examined, but the consequences of losing those alternatives should be understood before the agreement becomes binding.

Electrification makes this especially important. Charging equipment, substations and electricity connections involve different suppliers, construction schedules and contractual responsibilities from the buses themselves. Vehicle orders can proceed before chargers are fully commissioned when the infrastructure delivery pathway is sufficiently assured. Problems arise when a fleet commitment depends on electrical capacity that cannot be delivered in time, or when the fallback arrangements are inadequate.

The passenger network can also change in ways that alter the original investment case. Better bus priority can reduce the number of vehicles needed to maintain a timetable. New housing developments can shift demand toward different corridors. A major employment centre or hospital relocation can change the value of existing routes and depots. The infrastructure secured today should support those possibilities rather than make sensible network improvements prohibitively expensive.

None of this argues for delaying every investment until uncertainty disappears. Authorities need to secure land, procure vehicles and obtain electrical connections years before some services begin. The useful distinction is between preparation that reduces uncertainty and commitments that substantially increase the cost of changing direction. Both need to be assessed against the passenger services the authority intends to deliver.

West Yorkshire’s programme offers a concrete example of the opportunity and challenge. Securing assets and specifying passenger services across the metropolitan network may produce a more coherent system than leaving every operator to optimize its own routes and depots. The long-term measure of success will be whether the authority can continue improving that network through changing demand, successive contracts and further electrification without having to reconstruct infrastructure it has already paid to provide.

This assessment concludes my five-part series drawn from The Bus Is Not the System, an 83-page TFIE Strategy report examining four decades of British and Irish metropolitan bus governance. The full West Yorkshire Briefing connects the report’s findings to current fleet, depot, electricity infrastructure and franchising decisions.

#5793. Bulevirtide Linked to Less Decompensation in Chronic Hep D With Cirrhosis

— However, recently approved drug did not appear to reduce liver cancer risk in retrospective study

In patients with chronic hepatitis delta (CHD) with cirrhosis, treatment with bulevirtide (Hepcludex) was associated with lower risk of liver decompensation, according to results from a European retrospective study.

Among more than 700 CHD patients with cirrhosis, those treated with bulevirtide had significantly lower rates of de-novo decompensation compared with untreated patients, with 3-year cumulative incidence rates of 3% versus 11.3%, respectively (P=0.001), reported Elisabetta Degasperi, MD, PhD, of the Foundation IRCCS Ca' Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico in Milan.

On the other hand, there was no significant difference in 3-year de-novo hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) rates between the two cohorts (7.3% for treated patients vs 3.6% for untreated patients, P=0.86).

"In chronic hepatitis delta patients with cirrhosis, a 36-month course of bulevirtide monotherapy reduces decompensation, but not HCC, compared to historical pooled untreated cohorts," Degasperi said at the annual Liver Meeting in Denver, sponsored by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases.

"Chronic hepatitis delta is the most severe form of viral hepatitis, resulting in fast progression to cirrhosis and its complications, such as hepatocellular carcinoma and decompensation," Degasperi said, in explaining the rationale behind the study.

She pointed out that bulevirtide has been approved by the FDA for treatment of CHD in adults without cirrhosis or with compensated cirrhosis, and that in phase II and III clinical trials and real-world studies, bulevirtide monotherapy has achieved higher rates of virological and biochemical responses in patients with cirrhosis.

"However, the impact of bulevirtide treatment on hard clinical outcomes remains scarcely defined," she added.

Here, CHD patients with cirrhosis receiving bulevirtide monotherapy for up to 3 years in a retrospective European cohort study were compared with pooled data from two cohorts not treated with bulevirtide. The study endpoints were the incidence of liver-related events (decompensation and HCC), death, or liver transplantation.

The study included a total of 729 patients (431 treated with bulevirtide and 298 untreated controls). There were some significant differences in baseline characteristics between the cohorts (including age and sex), but inverse probability treatment weighing (IPTW) was used to balance the groups.

Among patients treated with bulevirtide monotherapy, 72% achieved virological response, 70% biochemical response, and 54% a combined response at 3 years.

During the course of the study, there were a total of 36 de novo liver-related events in bulevirtide-treated patients (12 decompensation and 24 HCC) and 32 in untreated patients (24 decompensation and eight HCC).

In the IPTW-adjusted Cox regression analysis, bulevirtide-treated patients had significantly lower risk of developing liver-related events compared with untreated controls (HR 0.69, 95% CI 0.49-0.99, P=0.04) or decompensation (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.44-0.98, P=0.03). These results were confirmed by the IPTW-adjusted competing risks regression model.

Conversely, the risk of HCC was similar between the two groups (HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.50-1.36, P=0.46).

Among patients treated with bulevirtide, lower baseline albumin values independently predicted liver decompensation (HR 0.17, 95% CI 0.07-0.39, P=0.001), while independent predictors of HCC in this group also included lower albumin (HR 0.22, 95% CI 0.11-0.44, P<0.001), as well as older age (HR 1.05, 95% CI 1.01-1.09, P=0.01) and male sex (HR 3.72, 95% CI 1.39-9.91, P=0.01).

Regarding overall survival (OS), "we did not see any significant difference between bulevirtide-treated and untreated patients, and this was also confirmed in the adjusted analysis," Degasperi observed. The 3-year OS rate was 95.2% with bulevirtide and 96.2% among untreated patients (P=0.63).

However, "if you concentrate on the features of events, we can see that most events leading to liver transplant, and also death, in the bulevirtide-treated cohort were HCC related, while in untreated patients, end-stage liver disease was the most frequent liver-related event leading to death and liver transplant," she pointed out.

Specifically, there were a total of 16 deaths or liver transplantations in the bulevirtide arm, 12 of which were HCC related, while seven of the nine deaths or liver transplantations in the untreated cohort were related to end-stage liver disease.

"Of course, additional studies in cohorts with extended follow-up are needed in order to confirm these data," she concluded.

Sierra Club and partner organizations have given the proposed Eversource pipeline the name “SERPent” to highlight its potential harm to public health, energy affordability, climate, and the Connecticut River which, if approved, the pipeline will run under.

Burning fossil gas kills people, disrupts the climate and makes energy unaffordable, but it has been very profitable for Eversource. The time for change is here.”

“As young people, we are critically aware of the fallacies embedded in the short-term logic of fossil fuel infrastructure,” said Jo Almond, Sunrise Movement Wesleyan. “I grew up in a town with one hundred and forty-four active methane gas leaks; a result of relying on natural gas pipelines imposed by our utility company. “Environmental racism harms all communities and it is important to hold corporations and utilities accountable for expanding poisonous methane gas into our communities and exposing us to environmental harms that exacerbate health, housing, education and economic barriers,” said Tenaya Taylor, Nonprofit Accountability Group.

#5791. I've Solved The 72-Hour EV Test Drive Conundrum, And Every Automaker Is Free To Steal My Idea (Except Tesla)

Because Republicans have fought so hard to spread pro-oil propaganda about electric vehicles, the general public largely has no idea whether an EV would work for them or not. Batteries easily last well over a decade and are recyclable, fast chargers are actually pretty common, and lifecycle emissions are way lower for EVs even if you account for mining, but somehow, objectively true statements are controversial now. New EV sales in the U.S. are also struggling, and automakers are struggling to find buyers. The good news is, I have an actual, viable solution that automakers are free steal borrow.

OK, so we've seen that spending time living with an EV, even temporarily, goes a long way to debunking pro-oil propaganda and can change people's minds about whether or not an EV is right for them. Personally, I think the easiest way to make that happen is for owners who want to see EVs get more popular to lend their cars to as many people as they can, for at least 3 days at a time. Ideally, automakers would offer 120-hour test drives to anyone who wants one, but that would be wildly expensive, so I understand why it's hard to even get a 72-hour loan.

Automakers can't sit back here, though. And I'm not just saying that because EVs are the future (they really are), or because I want my nieces and nephews to grow up breathing clean air (I really do). No, it's because they're already shipping EVs to the U.S., and selling more of them would help both sales and profits, while keeping excess inventory from piling up on dealer lots. So here's the idea I'm offering every automaker, free and clear: introduce incentives that encourage dealers to use EVs as service loaners.

When an auto journalist gives business advice, usually, the best thing any automaker can do is the opposite. And that goes double when that advice is on Jalopnik, a site that still loves a good s—post. I'm also well aware I'm not a serious journalist. But tell me the service loaner isn't the most cost-effective way to get customers into an EV long enough for them to realize how great it is to have a gas station in your garage.

I know we all love conquest sales, but current owners are your most likely future customers. The real key to a future EV sale, though, is the low-pressure, no-commitment, just-try-it-for-fun nature of the service loaner. Even people who actively hate EVs would probably be willing to play with one for three or four days while their car's in the shop if the loaner was free. Customers are less likely to think it's some sort of sales trick, too, if the offer comes from a service manager instead of a salesperson.

Considering we're talking about people who already own a car, I don't know if we'd see large numbers of owners picking up their cars, handing over the keys to the loaner EV, and demanding to trade their car in. But as long as you make a good car, there are no downsides to making a positive impression on your customers. And I bet that program would end up being the most cost-effective sales tool in any automaker's arsenal. Not because they're forcing people to go electric but because EVs do such a great job of selling themselves when they fit a prospective owner's lifestyle.

Not everyone can justify an EV. It's pricier and less convenient if you can't charge at home, and some people do crazy amounts of driving or frequent towing. But if you work for an automaker, you know your EVs make better daily drivers for regular homeowners than your most popular daily drivers, and you know they'd sell better if you could get more butts in seats. Now you have a way to get your most likely customers' butts in those seats for far less than the cost of launching a 120-hour test drive program.

Even better, the anti-EV crowd should be all over this one. If EVs are still as bad as they're convinced they are, then a few days driving an EV should be all anyone needs to disabuse them of the notion that they should go electric. Give the skeptics at your company the opportunity to rack up a win and prove this whole EV thing is a waste of everyone's time and money. I mean, they aren't afraid people will like EVs better if they just spend some time with one, are they? Let's put our money where our mouth is and find out.
