#5772. Healthcare Dealmakers—Chicago's $11B hospital merger, another health system ASC deal and more

Healthcare Dealmakers—Chicago's $11B hospital merger, another health system ASC deal and more" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Healthcare mergers and acquisitions are in no short supply as providers, health tech companies, payers and other industry players look to expand their businesses and gain a competitive edge. Here’s a roundup of new deals that were revealed, closed, rumored or called off during the month of October.

Rush University System for Health and Endeavor Health announced plans to merge, becoming a 12-hospital nonprofit with nearly $11 billion in annual revenue. The resulting entity would command over 400 care sites, employ more than 46,000 people including over 3,400 clinicians, and reach over 2 million Northern Illinois and Northwest Indiana patients per year. The pair are targeting an early 2027 close and outlined plans to commit $1 billion of Endeavor funds toward care in the region.

Private equity firm CD&R and healthcare conglomerate McKesson plan to acquire Option Care Health, a provider of infusion therapy services, in a deal valued at $5.8 billion. The purchase gives equity holders a per-share offer of $32.05 and is expected to close in the first half of 2027. CD&R would be the majority stakeholder in the company, which is the country’s largest independent at-home and alternate site infusion services provider.

Bon Secours Mercy Health announced plans to acquire a majority stake in Surgery Partners, among the country’s largest outpatient surgical care companies, in a take-private deal valuing the acquiree at $5.7 billion. Bain Capital Private Equity will roll over its 39% share of the company as it's purchased by a Bon Secours affiliate at $23.50 per share. Surgery Partners includes more than 200 locations and about 5,000 affiliated physicians across 30 states. The organizations are targeting an early 2027 close.

Risant Health, Kaiser Permanente’s subsidiary value-based care platform, announced Integris Health as its next regional health system acquisition. Financial terms were not disclosed, though the deal aims for an early 2027 close. Integris is Oklahoma’s largest nonprofit provider with 10 acute and 10 specialty hospitals with $3.3 billion in total operating revenues during the 2025 fiscal year.

MultiCare Health System picked up the final needed regulatory approval to absorb Samaritan Health Services during October. The nonprofits then consummated their 18-hospital combination on Nov. 1.

Hackensack Meridian Health has signed a definitive agreement to pick up Central New Jersey’s Hunterdon Health, which would grow the state’s largest health system to 19 total hospitals. The agreement outlines a $200 million capital investment from Hackensack Meridian, plus another $30 million to roll out Epic’s electronic health record.

Cencora (formerly AmerisourceBergen) signed a definitive agreement to acquire American Oncology Network, a collection of more than 350 oncology providers, in a deal valuing the network at $2.4 billion. Cencora said it expects to pay $1.7 billion to increase its 4% interest to 75%.

Parkview Health is acquiring Ovation Healthcare, a nationwide shared services vendor for providers. The 16-hospital Indiana nonprofit did not disclose financial terms, but said it hopes to close the deal within weeks. Parkview views the pickup as an opportunity to boost its administrative capabilities, which could be offered to other rural systems.

Parkview Health also wrapped its acquisition of Goshen Health, a 105-bed hospital with a network of physicians.

Independence Health System, a five-hospital nonprofit in western Pennsylvania, joined the West Virginia University Health System on Oct. 1. The deal was announced late last year and brings a five-year, $800 million capital commitment from WVU Health System toward the Independence hospitals and communities, which will "immediately" begin operating under the WVU Medicine brand.

Kettering Health plans to add Knox Community Hospital as its 15th medical center. The Ohio systems signed a definitive agreement for their deal, which will include undisclosed commitments toward Knox’s facilities, equipment and technology.

Nationwide Children’s Hospital plans to acquire the pediatric practice of Knox Community Hospital in spring 2027. Nationwide plans to combine the practice with one of its affiliates and continue providing services to Knox.

Allegiance Health Management said it plans to divest four Louisiana hospitals: Minden Medical Center, Northern Louisiana Medical Center, Acadian Medical Center and Mercy Regional Medical Center. No potential buyers or deal timelines were given.

Orlando Health closed its acquisition of RMC Health System, an Alabama organization with a 375-bed medical center. The deal was first announced in April, and brings five years of “significant” investment into RMC’s facilities, equipment and technology.

HCA Healthcare sold 31 home health and hospital agencies to Deaconess Associations. The facilities were located across eight states. Financial terms were not disclosed.

MaineHealth added York Hospital to its Southern region, marking the 79-bed facility as the system’s tenth hospital.

Ascension Seton said it is acquiring three locations in the greater Austin area from Family Health Systems, one of which is the Auton-based Family Hospital. The deal is set to close later this year.

Cone Health entered an agreement to acquire three pharmacies in Reidsville, North Carolina: Carolina Apothecary, Belmont Pharmacy and Rx Care.

Humana struck a deal shifting out Welsh, Carson, Anderson & Stowe for BlackRock for equity in a joint venture running about 150 of its CenterWell locations. The deal sees BlackRock buying out WCAS’ equity for about $2.8 billion.

Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield of New Jersey is acquiring the New Jersey operations of Summit Health, which includes CityMD urgent care sites. Financial details or a potential timeline were not disclosed.

Redesign Health plans to merge with Sheba Medical Center’s innovation arm, ARC Global, creating a roughly $2 billion company. The pair hope to build an end-to-end platform that helps health systems to turn ideas originating with their own clinicians and operators into technology products and standalone companies that can then be scaled across a global network. To help do so, the pair also agreed to acquire strategic advisory and intelligence firm AVIA.

Teladoc Health acquired Teledigm Health, which provides hybrid clinical services and specialized care support for rural and regional health systems, the public virtual care company announced alongside its Q3 earnings. Financial terms were not disclosed. Teladoc leadership said picking up its longtime partner will help it grow with providers serving rural communities.

RadNet, an imaging center operator and seller of radiology technology, is acquiring Onrad, a teleradiology services company with 130 contracted radiologists. The deal is expected to close early next year and will bring Onrad shareholders a collective $350 million plus 5 million RadNet shares, with additional performance-based earnouts.

iRhythm wrapped its acquisition of cardiac remote patient monitoring company VitalConnect for $237.5 million. The deal will help iRhythm evolve from ambulatory cardiac monitoring toward “a broader cardiac monitoring and intelligence platform,” its CEO and president told Fierce Healthcare.

Zocdoc acquired insurance technology company Sohar Health, the first acquisition in its nearly 20-year history and part of its push to evolve beyond an appointment-booking marketplace into broader healthcare access infrastructure. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Carenet Health, which provides patient engagement and navigation tools to over 400 healthcare partners, acquired Orbita, an AI engagement and communication company that does business with providers. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Tegria, a healthcare consultancy and services company, acquired cybersecurity, cloud hosting and managed IT services company CloudWave for an undisclosed sum.

Chapter, a Medicare navigation and retirement advisory company, has acquired Hively, a personalized retirement navigation and membership startup, for an undisclosed sum. The pair intend to launch in-person and online community programming for retirees surrounding retirement and aging topics, a move beyond Medicare navigation alone.

Sagility, a provider and payer technology services company, acquired Chirok Health, which offers clinical documentation improvement, medical coding and revenue integrity services for an undisclosed sum.

Investment firm Sopris Capital said it acquired Blackford Analysis, an AI medical imaging platform, from Bayer for an undisclosed sum. Sopris said it intends to deploy the company’s tools across its healthcare portfolio.

Emergence, a private equity firm, acquired digital intake and online reputation management software company Clinect for an undisclosed sum.

The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

Before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it says. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to users, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup

Schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. #5770. Safety of Controversial Vasculitis Drug Bolstered in Dedicated Trial

— Findings might help avacopan's fight to stay in the U.S. market

ORLANDO -- Interim results from a prospective trial designed to evaluate safety of avacopan (Tavneos), the embattled drug for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody-associated vasculitis (AAV), indicated that the product could still avoid total extinction.

Patients receiving avacopan in the trial, dubbed AvacoStar, experienced a fourfold higher rate of liver abnormalities compared with those treated instead with rituximab (Rituxan) or cyclophosphamide, as Bernhard Hellmich, MD, of the University of Tübingen in Germany, reported at the American College of Rheumatology's annual meeting.

However, these liver abnormalities were neither common nor severe, and other significant adverse effects were no more common with avacopan than with the standard-of-care alternatives.

The findings should be a welcome boost for avacopan, for which 2026 was a very bad year. When it was approved for AAV in 2021, this drug that targets the complement pathway was seen as a valuable addition to treatment options. AAV was treated historically with corticosteroids, despite the serious adverse effects that come with chronic use. Rituximab and cyclophosphamide then joined the armamentarium, but they carry safety risks as well.

Avacopan ran into trouble earlier this year when it was revealed that its original developer, ChemoCentryx, had results from the drug's pivotal registration trial "readjudicated" after unblinding, which shifted some patients from nonresponders to responders. The original findings indicated that the primary endpoint was missed; following the changes, it was achieved.

The appearance of data manipulation set off a firestorm. Liver abnormalities were a known issue with avacopan, but a label warning was considered enough to mitigate the risks. But when the readjudication was discovered, the FDA asked Amgen, which assumed control of avacopan in the U.S. after buying ChemoCentryx in 2022, to take the drug off the market voluntarily. The liver problems gained even more prominence in March when the FDA linked avacopan to eight deaths and 76 worldwide cases of drug-induced liver injury, including 54 hospitalizations.

Across the Atlantic, meanwhile, the controversy over data integrity in the pivotal trial prompted British and European regulators to order avacopan's withdrawal. Its marketing authorization was revoked in August in the European Union, while its withdrawal in the U.K. will be completed by this coming March.

Thus far, Amgen has rejected the FDA's withdrawal request, and the agency has not made it mandatory. Findings from the new safety study, along with an Italian study published last month that confirmed avacopan's efficacy in AAV, might be enough to keep the drug available in the U.S., at least for the time being.

AvacoStar was started in 2023 by Vifor Fresenius Medical Care Renal Pharma -- a joint venture between Fresenius Medical Care and what is now CSL Vifor, which had licensed avacopan from ChemoCentryx in Europe and felt a dedicated safety study was needed. The study enrolled 504 patients with highly active AAV in Britain and Germany who would be given either avacopan or one of the more conventional alternatives at clinicians' discretion, with 254 receiving avacopan and 250 an alternative regimen.

Outcomes were four types of "medical events of special interest," which included liver injury, cardiovascular events, serious infections, and malignancies -- altogether with 101 events in 72 patients (28.3%, 0.30 per patient-year). These were identified from participants' subsequent medical records. The study is still ongoing, with final completion scheduled in 2030. Hellmich's report involved data extracted as of September 2025, at which point more than 95% of patients were still on their original therapy, with mean duration of 16.2 months for avacopan and 12.7 months for the alternatives.

Mean patient age was about 64, and half of them were men. Specific AAV subtypes were equally split between granulomatosis with polyangiitis and microscopic polyangiitis. Almost three-quarters of patients were newly diagnosed. Half of them had serious renal impairment, including some 20% with estimated glomerular filtration rate less than 15 mL/min/1.73 m2.

Liver injury was the only medical event of special interest that was significantly more common with avacopan (IRR 4.03, 95% CI 1.55-10.48), and the absolute rate was reassuringly low, at 0.07 per patient-year (95% CI 0.05-0.10). Serious infections were the most common, at 0.14 per patient-year in the avacopan group, compared with 0.18 per patient-year with rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Cardiac events occurred at 0.09 per patient-year in both groups, and malignancies were also seen at equal rates, 0.02 per patient-year.

Most liver events with avacopan happened in the first 6 months of treatment, Hellmich said. Of the 22 such events overall, 10 were considered by treating clinicians to be probably or definitely unrelated to the drug. Among the 12 cases considered possibly, probably, or certainly due to avacopan, three continued with their regular dosing and five stopped it temporarily.

Hellmich also emphasized that 20 of the 22 cases had resolved before the interim data cut. One of the other two was reported to have been resolved later, while the last had not but, Hellmich said, was thought to be "clinically irrelevant."

With regard to study limitations, he cautioned that, because site investigators chose treatments based on their own judgments, "residual bias" is a possibility. As well, final results with additional years of treatment might reveal risks not yet apparent.

#5769. How A Salesman Accidentally Convinced Shaquille O'Neal To Buy 3 Ridiculously Expensive Cars

Shaquille O'Neal doesn't do small or understated. The 7-foot-1 four-time NBA champion has an instantly recognizable brand. Oh, he's worth around $500 million, too. Naturally, as with many other well-to-do star athletes, he has a penchant for flashy cars. Problem is, he seldom fits in them without some contortions and modification. It's what drove him to have a Lamborghini lengthened into a Franken-Gallardo. That stretched supercar isn't the only time Shaq did some silly stuff with expensive cars.

In what was almost certainly a prideful purchase, O'Neal bought three outrageously expensive cars on the spot. Why? All it took was one condescending question from a less-than-respectful Rolls-Royce dealership salesman, and Shaq bought the lot. Just like that, the champ and business mogul had three extra opulent cars he says "I never drive."

Don't believe it? One of them, a 2004 Rolls-Royce Phantom, just sold on Bring-a-Trailer. If that wasn't enough, the once-undisputed heavyweight champion of the world, Mike Tyson, may have had a hand in nudging the Diesel to buy three ultraluxe cars instead of a solitary sedan. Of course, it's not difficult to get carried away when shopping for Rolls-Royces; just look at the one-off Phantom inspired by "Goldfinger."

Some 30 years ago, Shaquille O'Neal signed a groundbreaking $120 million deal to don Los Angeles Lakers colors and put away his Orlando Magic jersey. Several years later, he wandered into a Rolls-Royce showroom with his friend Alex and started browsing the hand-built grandeur.

Now, O'Neal had money to spare, but he wasn't quite up for indiscriminate spending. "I like to spend money, but I don't like to waste money. So I don't want to spend $400,000 for a car," O'Neal recalled in a Revolt interview. He went about asking a salesperson about the prices of the showroom's many Roll-Royces. That's when the salesperson said the wrong thing. Or the right thing, considering the commission on three hilariously expensive cars.

In O'Neal's book, "Shaq Uncut: My Story,"  he recalls the question as especially disrespectful, be it accidental or deliberate. The salesperson gave the Lakers sweatpants-clad O'Neal a glance and, per Basketball Network, asked, "Are you sure you can afford it, sonny boy?" That did it. Shaq lost it. "I said, 'What the f*** did you just say to me?'" So, he pointed around the showroom. "I want that silver hardtop one, and I want the green one, and give that red one over there, too."

One of those cars, the silver hardtop O'Neal selected, was a 2004 Rolls-Royce Phantom. That car sold in November 2026 on Bring-a-Trailer for $62,000. Not exactly the $320,000 or so O'Neal likely paid for it when it was new in 2004. Although he was shopping in a Rolls-Royce dealer, Shaq's book mentions a handful of Bentleys as part of the splurge. Whichever British luxury marque made O'Neal's list of picks, it was quite the spendy visit to a dealership.

Shaq's financial flexing and what is likely the most impressive commission that Rolls-Royce salesperson has ever made makes for a pretty crazy story. Believe it or not, it gets even more wild from there. According to O'Neal's book, "Iron" Mike himself, Mike Tyson, was in the mood for Bentley shopping just as the Laker found himself at the dealership.

Shaq recalled seeing Tyson picking out a couple of Bentleys and the need to out-do the champion pugilist. "Next thing I know Tyson picked out two. He's buying two of these cars, so you know what I've got to do. I've got to buy three!" Though it's not clear what ratio of Rolls-Royce to Bentleys made up his impulse shopping spree.

Be it Iron Mike or the mouthy salesperson who drove Shaq to pull the trigger, the outlandishly expensive price tag for the purchase hit him after. "A million dollars gone in 10 minutes," the massive athlete once lamented in an interview with Vanity Fair. Frankly, that's not the only time O'Neal has had the rotten luck with luxury cars. After spending the money to have it customized to fit his considerable frame, his Lucid Air Coupe ended up in a salvage yard less than two years later. Bummer.

#5768. A Tribute to Bunker Roy: The Man Who Turned Village Grandmothers into Solar Engineers

Sanjit “Bunker” Roy, who taught illiterate grandmothers to become solar engineers, passed away peacefully this morning at his home in Tilonia, Rajasthan, aged 81.[1] I first encountered his work not in India, but in the rain forests of Borneo.

It was October 2016, and as night fell, the surrounding Borneo tropical rain forest had come alive with noise, dominated by the trill of frogs and the rhythmic pulse of cicadas. I was about to embark on the Sabah study tour of the Emerging Leaders Dialogue Asia (ELDA). Over the next two weeks, we would visit timber plantations, mountain communities recovering from a deadly earthquake, and marine parks.

But undoubtedly the highlight for me was discovering the inspiring story of Barefoot College, which trains village grandmothers to be solar engineers. On our first evening, while enjoying a mini feast of banana fritters, pomelo, and langsat (a bit like lychees but more delicious), we were told about the college’s remarkable partnership with the Sabah Women Entrepreneurs and Professionals Association (SWEPA) in Borneo.

Barefoot College was the brainchild of Bunker Roy, and he was an unlikely revolutionary. Born into privilege in Bengal in 1945, he was educated at the Doon School and St Stephen’s College, Delhi—two of India’s most elite institutions—and was a national squash champion. A conventional career beckoned. Then, during the Bihar famine of the mid-1960s, he saw rural poverty firsthand, and his life changed course.[2] When he told his mother he wanted to live and work in a village, he later joked, she “went into a coma” and didn’t speak to him for a long time.[3]

In 1972, Roy settled in Tilonia, a dusty village in Rajasthan, and founded the Social Work and Research Centre (SWRC), which later became known as Barefoot College. Its rules turned conventional education on its head. Anyone with a university degree was disqualified from studying there, and no degrees were awarded. In 2011, Roy said that nobody at the college earned more than $100 a month. The campus itself was built in 1986 by a dozen local “barefoot architects” who could not read or write, and it went on to win an Aga Khan Award for Architecture. At the college’s night schools, children aged 6 to 14 elect their own prime minister and cabinet.[4]

Roy’s guiding conviction was simple: “There is no urban solution to a rural problem.”[5] He was awarded the Padma Shri, one of India’s highest civilian honors, in 1986, and named one of Time magazine’s 100 most influential people in 2010.[6] He is survived by his wife, Aruna Roy, the former civil servant who led the grassroots movement behind India’s Right to Information Act.[7]

The positive impact of his work has been immense. By the college’s own count at its 50th anniversary in 2022, it had trained 1,708 illiterate and semi-literate rural women from 96 countries as solar engineers, bringing light to more than a million people in over 75,000 households and saving about 45 million liters of kerosene. Its rainwater harvesting had captured some 70 billion liters and brought safe drinking water to more than 1,650 schools. More than 90,000 working children had studied in its night schools, and its barefoot health workers had treated over 300,000 patients.[8]

During our study tour, SWEPA arranged for us to meet one of Barefoot College’s beneficiaries, a so-called solar mama. She was part of the program that takes illiterate grandmothers from poor rural villages and, within six months, trains them at the college in India for their new job. They return to their villages to install and maintain full solar lighting systems. Roy deliberately chose grandmothers because they are rooted in their communities; men and younger people, he found, were more likely to take their new skills and leave for the city.[9] Because the women shared no common language, much of the training was done through sign language and hands-on practice.[10]

Malaysia’s first solar mama—very likely the woman I met that evening—was Tarihing Masanim, from Kampung Sonsogon Magandai, near Kota Marudu in Sabah. She completed her training in India in 2015 and returned to bring electricity to around 100 homes in her village.[11] Roy loved to tell stories like hers. One of his favorites was about a 55-year-old Afghan grandmother who electrified 200 houses and set an Afghan engineering department head straight on the difference between AC and DC.[12]

The story of the solar mamas captures many elements of what it means to harness the power of responsibility to create a more inclusive society and economy. So many barriers are being broken through, as these amazing women challenge stereotypes about age, gender, and rural capacity. Barefoot College shows that sustainable development—including adopting sustainable technologies—is an option for people living with low incomes in remote villages. The Barefoot model empowers people to be agents of their own destiny.

Bunker Roy stands out as an inspiring example of inclusive leadership. His impact, which is so strongly evidenced by the solar engineers program, is as much about restoring dignity to those who are traditionally excluded as it is about developing or transferring practical skills. Roy, who said he had “a very elitist, snobbish, expensive education in India” that “almost destroyed” him, explained:

“So we started the Barefoot College, and we redefined professionalism. Who is a professional? A professional is someone who has a combination of competence, confidence and belief. A water diviner is a professional. A traditional midwife is a professional. A traditional bone setter is a professional. These are professionals all over the world. You find them in any inaccessible village around the world. And we thought that these people should come into the mainstream and show that the knowledge and skills that they have is universal.”[13]

Roy ended that talk with a line often attributed to Mahatma Gandhi, whose principles guided his life’s work: “First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, and then you win.”[14] For the solar mamas of Barefoot College, and for the more than a million people whose homes they have lit, Bunker Roy won.

#5767. Experience The Gales Of November With This Real-Time Great Lakes Simulator

The wreck of the SS Edmund Fitzgerald became a bit of a meme last year during the 50th anniversary of the disaster. Gen Zers rediscovered the great Gordon Lightfoot song and it was all over the interwebz. Those youths can now experience the thrill, terror and wonder of the Great Lakes firsthand with my new favorite obsession, the website In The Lakes; a free site which shows you the real-time conditions on any one of the great lakes without tracking your data.

Using buoys located on Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Huron, Lake Erie, and Lake Ontario and honorable mention Lake St. Claire, In The Lake users can view a digital simulation of conditions. Different colors on the map represent real-time wave heights. As of the writing of this story, both Lake Superior and Lake Michigan are mostly red, indicative of choppy waters and waves reaching 10 feet or more. My first "Float" sent me just north of Sault Ste. Marie in Lake Superior where it was, predictably, cold, grey, and extra choppy — just the sort of thing the Edmund Fitz faced on that cold day in November, 1975.

But it's not all rough seas and wind. Pick a calmer section of lake and spend a few hours of your work day sipping a beverage, listening to a radio that features local radio stations as well as multiple genre stations, or meditate. The meditate feature is fairly entertaining, with inspirational messages meant to resonant with folks from the Great Lakes. The last time I pressed it, a message popped up reading "Somewhere, someone's shoveling a driveway. Not you. Not today." Damn right.

But it's not just floaties. You can find the option to "Take the helm in these conditions." And the familiar lake scene will load with a kayak, schooner, or even a Coast Guard ice breaking ship. I tried out the kayak to see what it was like for my husband when he puttered around Lake Superior on his own kayak, a feat that nearly killed him. You can also dive the depths of the lakes, or write a message and pop it in a bottle, then set it into the lake and see where the real forecast takes it.

In the Experiences tab you can take on several adventures from repairing the Cort for sailing duties to Cruising the Soo Locks. There's also a plethora of adventures to go on. I opted for the Brigade to the Rendezvous, an 1815 canoe trip to deliver beaver furs to Fort William, a midway trading point between the Midwest and Montreal. Teachers can also find a dedicated hub with tons of resources to go over critical things related to the Great Lakes, appropriate for certain grade levels.

Or keep it simple and continue to enjoy the occasional float on one of the Great Lakes. You can use it to escape your kids as easily as educate them, after all. An extra click will allow your setting to reset (change) every five minutes without your interference. So relax, ride the waves, and beware the gales of November.

#5766. Equiti acquires Lexi AI to combine AI, human medical interpretation

Equiti acquires Lexi AI to combine AI, human medical interpretation" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Equiti is acquiring Lexi AI to build a hybrid language-access model that combines AI language support with human medical interpreters.

Equiti, which sells medical interpretation services to hospitals and health systems through its Martti business, provides 24/7 access to qualified medical interpreters across more than 250 languages and dialects. Lexi provides multilingual, AI-powered medical interpretation. The acquisition deal merges Lexi's immediate AI language support, covering over 35 languages and dialects, with Martti and its network of qualified medical interpreters to help healthcare organizations expand language access.

The acquisition was announced October 28. Financial details of the deal were not disclosed.

With this acquisition, Equiti is building on Martti’s work pioneering video remote interpretation in healthcare more than two decades ago, according to executives. The use of AI can expand where and when language services can be offered, particularly for everyday interactions that may not currently receive interpretation support, Equiti executives said.

Martti was built alongside healthcare organizations to make qualified interpreters available by video. Lexi, in turn, has been developed with healthcare customers to extend immediate language support into more workflows. The acquisition brings those capabilities together, with human-in-the-loop design, patient safety and patient experience at its center, Equiti executives said.

The company saw an opportunity to combine its services with Lexi's AI expertise rather than build a healthcare AI interpretation product internally, Maureen Huber, Equiti CEO, told Fierce Healthcare.

"Lexi brings specialized expertise in AI, engineering and healthcare product design, along with experience putting that technology into the hands of care teams. That combination takes time to build," Huber said. "For more than 20 years, our work through Martti has been about making qualified human interpretation accessible within healthcare. We understand the service, the clinical environment and what it takes to support healthcare organizations every day. Developing AI and machine learning technology calls for additional, specialized expertise. We wanted people who had already been doing that work with healthcare in mind."

She added, "We spent time evaluating the category and learning from customers. Lexi brought together the people, product and approach we were seeking. Combining their expertise with ours gives us a stronger foundation to expand language access responsibly."

Combining AI and human interpretation makes language support more accessible across the patient journey, helping organizations improve care delivery while making better use of their resources, according to Equiti executives.

Healthcare organizations are increasingly interested in AI interpretation capabilities and are looking for guidance, Huber noted.

"Customers were asking: 'Where could AI help? How do we evaluate it? What is appropriate for our patients?' Healthcare leaders see the same advances in consumer AI that everyone else sees. They also must think about what happens when those tools enter a care environment, sometimes before an organization has decided how they should be used. They want a partner who understands both the possibilities and the responsibilities," she said.

She added, "I would describe that as inquiry and evaluation. There is real curiosity about extending language support to more of the patient experience, particularly before and after a visit. Our job is to help customers identify those opportunities while keeping qualified human interpretation central to care delivery."

Equiti calls this approach Modality Matters, a connected model that allows healthcare organizations to match each encounter with the appropriate modality — immediate, healthcare-purpose-built AI support for approved use cases and qualified medical interpretation where clinical complexity, regulatory requirements, organizational policy or patient preference calls for a human interpreter. With this approach, organizations have the flexibility to shift between modalities as clinical context and communication needs change in real time.

The combined portfolio of Equiti and Lexi's capabilities will extend language access into everyday interactions that often go unsupported, Huber noted.

Equiti is focusing Lexi's AI-powered medical interpretation on routine patient engagement, including before and after care, such as appointment communications, scheduling and nonclinical follow-up logistics.

"We see a significant opportunity for Lexi in that communication before and after care: helping patients exchange messages, arrange appointments and stay connected in their preferred language. Language access must extend beyond the clinical encounter. Think about what happens after a patient leaves the clinic. They receive a message about a follow-up appointment, but they need to ask whether it is at the same location, how to reschedule, or whom to contact. Those may be simple questions for the organization, but the answers determine whether the patient can take the next step," she said.

Qualified human interpreters remain the foundation for care delivery, Huber noted. "In conversations such as those about a diagnosis, informed consent, treatment or palliative care, the ability to clarify meaning, recognize cultural context and respond with empathy is essential. A medically qualified interpreter helps people understand one another through conversations that can be complex and deeply personal," she said.

Equiti said it can work with customers to define appropriate uses within their policies and applicable requirements, preserving patient choice and access to a qualified human interpreter.

Language access is also a strategic performance driver for healthcare organizations, as effective communication influences patient understanding and experience, clinical outcomes, workforce efficiency and financial performance.

Equiti's customers include Wellstar Health System, Corewell Health, NYU Langone and Lee Health. Lexi works with a growing pipeline of federally qualified health centers and community providers including Lowell Community Health Center, which serves one of the most multilingual communities in Massachusetts.

As general-purpose AI gets better at translation, a healthcare-specific interpretation platform has distinct advantages, Huber asserted.

"Healthcare communication involves clinical meaning, cultural context, jargon and acronyms during situations where people may be frightened, vulnerable or unsure how to ask a question. Our job is to remove those communication barriers, and that requires understanding the care environment, fitting into clinical workflows and knowing when a qualified human interpreter needs to be involved," she said. "That is where Equiti’s experience matters. We bring the relationships, service infrastructure and human expertise developed through more than two decades of healthcare interpretation, alongside Lexi’s technology and team."

Huber said she envisions broader uses of Lexi's AI language support in healthcare workflows. "A patient’s need to communicate continues after the conversation with a clinician ends. Lexi already supports text-based messaging, including translation of text provided by a care team, and can even leave voicemail messages for patients. That creates opportunities to help patients access information and communicate between visits. Helping someone navigate follow-up care is a natural direction for that work, like understanding the next step, connecting with the right office or arranging an appointment. The value is in making it easier for patients to act on the care plan they have been given and ask for help along the way," she said.

"We built Lexi to fit the way healthcare teams actually work, bringing immediate language support into the devices and workflows they already use,” Siddharth UR, co-founder and chief product officer of Lexi, said in a statement. “As part of Equiti, we can extend that experience across the patient journey and connect it to a broader language access model built around the needs of each encounter.”

Lexi will operate alongside Martti under Equiti, with the teams working together on implementation and integration across healthcare workflows. Equiti will work with each customer to determine how the solutions fit within its language access program, clinical environment, and organizational policies.

#5765. Oh, So That’s Who’s Buying All Those New Subaru Trailseeker EVs…

After EV sales in the US crashed into a brick wall last year, the Subaru Trailseeker has been one of the few points of light. Newly introduced this year, Trailseeker has racked up a relatively decent sales track record in the crowded SUV field. As for whether or not Subaru can continue to grow its EV sales in the US, the automaker’s elaborate, multi-faceted “Subaru Loves Pets” campaign has emerged as the secret weapon…

The Subaru Loves Pets campaign first appeared 18 years ago, back in 2008. A lot of demographic and cultural water has passed under the bridge since then. More so than in past generations, pets have taken on the role of family members equal to, if not superior to, anyone else in the household. And if that’s the case, shouldn’t pets have their own seatbelts, too?

Now Subaru’s longtime relationship with the pet-centered population is beginning to muscle into EV territory. One indication of a connection between pet and EV preferences surfaced in October, when Subaru released a new report indicating that pets wield a noticeable influence on purchasing  preferences in the US auto market overall.

Commissioned from the firm Talker Research, the report is based on interviews with 2,000 and pet owners in the US. Of that cohort, a resounding majority of 73% said they are more likely to drive for the holidays, specifically in order to travel with their pet.

“As the holidays approach, more than two-thirds (68%) said their pet will affect their travel plans this year, and nearly half (45%) have turned down travel opportunities that couldn’t accommodate their pet,” Subaru adds.

Households with pets also have distinct priorities for a vehicle. “Plenty of room between pets, passengers, and luggage tops the list of features pet owners say matter when traveling with an animal,” Suburu reports.

“More than one in four (26%) prioritize cargo space for crates, carriers, beds, or gear. Among hybrid and EV drivers, that climbs to 35%,” the automaker further notes.

If you missed the money quote, it’s that thing about 35% of hybrid and EV drivers prioritizing space for pet gear, compared to just 26% of drivers overall. In addition to the traveling-with-pets angle, that generational difference also reflects a sharp generational divergence in attitudes towards EVs.

“Electric vehicles have become a political flashpoint in Washington. But new national polling finds the biggest divide among potential EV buyers isn’t political. It’s generational,” reports the advocacy organization ZETA (the Zero Emission Transportation Association) in September.

“Seventy-five percent of adults ages 18–34 and 72% of adults ages 35–49 say they are likely to purchase or lease a new EV within the next five years,” ZETA elaborates. “Among adults ages 50–64, that number falls to 50%. Among those 65 and older, it drops to just 23%, a striking 52-point gap between the youngest and oldest Americans.”

Now let’s take another look at the Subaru survey. Talker Research found that 75% of Gen Z and 70% of millennials traveled with a pet within the past five years, compared with just 58% of Gen X and only 40% of baby boomers (looking at you, Mitt Romney).

A similar generational difference surfaced in other areas of the survey:

Younger pet owners are also more likely to say they plan travel around their pet, with 42% of Gen Z and millennials doing so compared with 27% of Gen X and boomers.

Among pet owners who haven’t yet road-tripped with their pet, 74% of Gen Z and millennials would consider it, compared with 54% of Gen X and boomers.

Subaru pulled back on its overall electrification plan for the US market after last year’s EV sales crash, but it did follow through on the new Trailseeker, offered for sale on a limited basis in January of this year. Volume deliveries to dealers began in April of this year, and in May the Trailseeker racked up 1,074 in sales. The number is vanishingly small compared to industry leader Tesla but a promising start in the challenging US market. By August, Trailseeker had a total of almost 5,000 in sales for the year to its credit, rising to 6,006 sold by the end of October.

All else being equal, recognition from Wards Auto may help keep the momentum going. On October 13, Subaru announced that the Trailseeker earned a slot in the 2026 Wards 10 Best Engines & Propulsion Systems list.

“For 2026, Wards evaluated 26 powertrains from returning winners as well as all-new or significantly updated cars, trucks, or SUVs. They were evaluated on several criteria, including power, torque, refinement, efficiency, and innovation,” Subaru notes.

“Its 375 horsepower combined with immediate electric powertrain response always satisfies. Its range estimates also hold up well in real-world driving, interstate and all. Yet Subaru keeps the price completely reasonable given such capability,” said Robin Warner, who manages the 10 Best Engines & Propulsion Systems program.

By “completely reasonable,” Warner means the Trailseeker’s starting MSRP of $39,995 and its estimated range of 281 miles. According to Subaru, the Trailseeker can go from 10% to 80% charged in as little as 28 minutes, with up to 150 kW on a DC-fast charger.

“With an onboard battery preconditioning system, enabled either by navigating to a charging destination or by the driver via touchscreen controls, the Trailseeker can charge its battery in cold climates — as low as 14 degrees Fahrenheit — at speeds comparable to those in normal weather conditions,” Subaru also advises.

In addition to the seal of approval from Wards, on October 29 Subaru announced that Trailseeker earned the “Car of the Year” award in the 2027 TopGear.com US Car Awards program

The automaker cites Top Gear US Correspondent Alex Kalogiannis, who was particularly enthused about the vehicle’s off-road performance. ““Off the beaten path, the set-and-forget X-MODE figures out all the tricky terrain stuff as you trundle through the bush, and with about 8.5 inches of ground clearance, it can scale all but the scariest obstacles in your path,” Kalogiannis remarked, somwhat colorfully.

“People still carry a torch for the WRX and its many rally-inspired incarnations, but the heart of Subaru fandom now is its dutiful, rugged, useful wagon – the Trailseeker,” he added.

That remains to be seen. Trailseeker will have to compete for the hearts and minds of Subaru fans against other models in the automaker’s lineup, including gasmobiles. The SUV-styled Outback wagon, for example, clocked 118,470 in sales from January to the end of October this year, and that was not the only Subaru model to hit six figures.

Still, US President Donald Trump has provided Subaru and other automakers with a new opportunity grow their EV sales profile this year. On February 28 the President launched his war against Iran, sending global oil prices on an upwards trajectory and improving the affordability case for EVs regardless of the loss of the $7,500 federal EV tax credit, which Trump and his Republican majority in Congress axed last fall.

Ever since dropping the first bombs on Iran, Trump has repeatedly claimed that the war is over, or almost over, or over any minute. In the latest pronouncement, on  Monday Trump said that multilateral negotiations over a peace settlement in Iran are in a state of “positive momentum toward an end.” And if you believe that…

#5764. Trial Stopped Early for Superiority of LBBP-Tuned Pacemakers

— LBBP preserved cardiac function and reduced events for people with AV block in randomized trial

Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) drastically reduced clinical events among patients with atrioventricular (AV) block, with results good enough to stop the OptimPacing trial early.

In that international randomized trial of patients getting permanent pacemakers with high ventricular pacing burden and a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) >35%, LBBP bested right ventricular pacing (RVP) when it came to the primary endpoint of combined mortality, heart failure hospitalization, or pacing-induced cardiomyopathy at an interim 35.1-month analysis.

The 4-year estimated Kaplan-Meier event rates were 8.5% and 19.2%, respectively (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.23-0.75), reported Jiangang Zou, MD, PhD, of First Affiliated Hospital, Nanjing Medical University, and Westchina Hospital in China. Individual outcomes were also reported for:

Safety-wise, procedure- and pacing system-related complications reached 3.8% and 3.2% in the LBBP and RVP groups, and lead revision occurred in two patients each, Zou reported at the American Heart Association (AHA) annual meeting held in Chicago.

"LBBP demonstrated superiority over RVP in preserving cardiac function and reducing composite clinical outcomes for atrioventricular block," Zou said. "This study provides evidence supporting the consideration of LBBP as a first-line pacing strategy for patients with an anticipated high ventricular pacing requirement."

OptimPacing was simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine.

LBBP is a type of conduction system pacing directly engaging the heart's intrinsic conduction system to preserve left ventricular electrical and mechanical synchrony. The result is typically a lower risk of pacing-induced cardiomyopathy -- compared with forced ventricular pacing -- hence LBBP becoming very popular in real-world practice.

"What we've learned here from this clinical trial, as we've learned when we buy a car or buy a house, is that location, location, location is very important," said Elaine Wan, MD, of Columbia University Medical Center in New York City, discussing the trial during a press conference.

LBBP in OptimPacing meant fixing a 3830 lumenless lead into the interventricular septum until the left ventricular subendocardium was reached, meeting prespecified LBBP criteria, whereas RVP meant a conventional active lead implanted in the right ventricular septum or apex using standard technique.

"Getting there and actually getting the effect, specifically the QRS that is similar to a physiological native QRS, is the goal, so not just parking it there, but actually getting the electrophysiological effect," Wan stressed. From OptimPacing's electrophysiological results of LBBP, "we get the most maintenance and sustainability of ejection fraction so far, since we've known for so long that forced ventricular pacing does not have any beneficial effect."

In 2023, the Heart Rhythm Society guidelines gave cardiac physiologic pacing a class IIa recommendation for patients with an LVEF 36-50% anticipated to require substantial ventricular pacing, and a weaker IIb recommendation for peers with normal LVEF anticipated to require substantial ventricular pacing.

Wan posed the question of whether it's time for a guideline change in the wake of OptimPacing.

"I do think that with the advent of septal left bundle pacing, definitely a lot of electrophysiologists are comfortable with the procedure," she added.

"I think that most of us are using left bundle branch area pacing as the default option," said press conference moderator Cara Pellegrini, MD, of the University of California San Francisco and VA San Francisco. "The rare times that you may still use right atrial right ventricular apical pacing might be if you were struggling with a left bundle area pacing lead and your patient was particularly sick, and you were just trying to do kind of the fastest, most expedient option."

Wan emphasized patient selection and noted that it is also unclear if people with infiltrative heart disease (e.g. amyloidosis) get the same effects from septal LBBP or RVP in someone with a normal heart.

Zou and colleagues conducted the randomized trial in China, Europe, and the U.S. from 2021-2025. The study population consisted of people with an indication for permanent pacemakers with a high ventricular pacing burden, LVEF >35%, and New York Heart Association class I-III symptoms.

Among exclusion criteria were candidates for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), or CRT-defibrillator therapy; and people with LVEF 36-50% who were willing to receive biventricular pacing.

The open-label trial had 702 patients randomized and 685 included in the final analysis. The two groups shared balanced baseline characteristics. Mean age was 68.4 years and 57.5% were men. Mean LVEF was 63%, and mean QRS duration about 115 msec. The indication for permanent pacing was atrial fibrillation with a slow ventricular rate in 12.7% of the cohort.

Pacing-induced cardiomyopathy was defined as a 10% or larger drop in LVEF and resultant LVEF ≤50% without alternative causes of cardiomyopathy identified. Heart failure hospitalization covered hospital admissions for more than 24 hours with worsening symptoms of heart failure and treatment with IV diuretics or inotropic medications.

LBBP was successfully implanted in 96.8% of patients; left bundle branch capture was confirmed in 87.6%.

The ventricular pacing burden was >90% in both groups.

Left ventricular end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes were lower with LBBP; LVEF was higher with LBBP.

R-wave sensing and pacing impedance and threshold remained stable in both groups. Left bundle branch capture threshold also remained low and stable, per Zou's report.

Key limitations of OptimPacing include its early termination, which may have led to an overestimation of treatment effects, and the low representation of people with reduced LVEF.

#5763. Omada Health hikes 2026 outlook after ‘strongest quarter ever’ in Q3

Omada Health hikes 2026 outlook after ‘strongest quarter ever’ in Q3" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Omada Health saw its "strongest quarter ever" in the third quarter of 2026, CEO and co-founder Sean Duffy told investors and analysts during a Thursday evening earnings call.

"We delivered our highest quarterly revenue, gross margin progression, and our most profitable quarter to date," Duffy said.

The virtual chronic care provider, which went public last June, brought in $91 million in revenue—up 34% year-over-year—and reported gross margin of 76% on a GAAP basis and 78% on a non-GAAP basis, according to Duffy. Omada reported net income of $7 million in the third quarter, compared with a net loss of $3 million in Q3 2025.

The company also reported adjusted EBITDA of $12 million, compared to $2 million the year prior.

It beat Wall Street analysts’ estimates for revenue, though slightly trailed behind projections for total membership.

Total members reached 1.1 million, up 36% year-over-year, with trailing 12-month revenue per total member increasing 5% year-over-year to $294, according to financial results published Thursday. Average member tenure also grew 10% compared to the year prior, to approximately two years and four months. Member retention has improved to 58%, up from 43% in Q4 of 2024, executives said.

Omada Health President Wei-Li Shao said Q3 membership growth reflects "continued demand" for its cardiometabolic platform, adding that the company's diabetes and hypertension programs continued to lead growth.

The company's diabetes and hypertension programs, longer member retention and lower care delivery costs are increasingly driving both growth and profitability, executives said.

"Members stayed with us longer, and our ability to provide personalized care at scale reached a new level of efficiency," Shao said.

The company supports diabetes, hypertension, obesity and musculoskeletal conditions—launching a GLP-1 care companion solution last November.

Shao noted that Omada deepened its partnership with the Health Care Services Corporation (HCSC) last quarter to extend its prevention and hypertension programs into three additional states, which is expected to "potentially reach an additional estimated 1.5 million covered lives at launch in 2027."

"On the PBM side, we have commercial relationships with the three largest PBMs in the country, which together processed an estimated 80% of prescription claims in 2025," Shao said. "Our prescribing program is in the market now at Optum. These relationships give us the broadest distribution in Omada’s history for our programs."

Shao, who will take over as CEO Jan. 1, also noted that artificial intelligence solutions enable care teams to have more capacity to "apply their clinical expertise" while tailoring care to each member’s needs.

"This quarter shows what we have built at Omada," Shao said. "Our commercial relationships give us broad reach, and our cardiometabolic programs have driven growth. Our program mix has supported longer member tenure, and our cost to serve has decreased."

Chief Financial Officer Steve Cook told investors the company expects new enrollments to "moderate sequentially" in the fourth quarter, which he said is "consistent with historic seasonality."

Shao also noted that a number of employers have been spending more time making GLP-1 coverage and obesity care decisions, "given the size of the commitment, the range of solutions and the importance of getting these decisions right," which has extended the selling season deeper into the fourth quarter.

Omada Health's stock dropped 19% Friday following the Q3 earnings call on Thursday as investors pulled back due to concerns about the longer selling season and expected Q4 member decline clouding the company's 2027 outlook.

The company is raising its full 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA outlook. Cook said revenue is expected to range from $344 million to $346 million, up from its previous range of $334 million to $340 million. Adjusted EBITDA is expected to be in the range of $32 million to $34 million, up from $21 million to $27 million.

"Our outlook anticipates Q4 revenue below our Q3 level, reflecting the lower new enrollment and engagement activity we have historically seen during the holidays," Cook said. "We expect revenue to come primarily from continued engagement among existing members."

#5762. At $14,000, Is This 1993 Toyota MR2 A Red-Hot Deal?

According to its seller, today's Nice Price or No Dice MR2 is a highly optioned model and was once sold on Bring a Trailer. It's been demoted to a Facebook Marketplace ad, and it's up to us to decide whether its price matches that lower-tier venue.

Rumored federal rollover safety standards effectively killed off convertible production in the U.S. from 1976 to the early '80s. The convertibles that boldly remained on the market during this time were all older cars like the MGB and Mercedes-Benz SL.

It was that latter convertible, the two-seater Benz, that served as the role model for the 1977 Cadillac Seville Milan we looked at on Monday. A custom-bodied two-seater convertible, the Milan attempted to fill that obvious gap in North America's car lineup. Unfortunately, the car's odd proportions gave the impression that upon arrival, its occupants would be revealed to be a congress of clowns rather than a chic couple with wind-tousled hair. That factor, plus questions about the car's condition, made us all question the seller's set $8,000 asking price. In short order, that dropped in an 82% 'No Dice' loss.

When it comes to styling and proportions, it's safe to say that Toyota hit the mark with the second-generation MR2. Larger, more cohesive, and roomier, the SW20 edition traded the first MR2's odd mini-Ferrari Mondial look for one more reverent to the better-looking Ferrari 328 GTB. It still checked all the boxes that made the first generation popular: a mid-engine layout, pop-up headlamps, and an optional T-top roof. Where the second-generation car strayed from the first was in size (it's substantially larger in almost all dimensions), and in the breathing of its top-models as the earlier cars' supercharger was traded for a turbo. One other distinction of the SW20 (perhaps unfairly) is that its handling at the limit can bite unwary drivers on the butt.

This 1993 MR2 comes in the officially named Super Red, making it a perfect accompaniment to the Man of Steel's cape and booties. This is a non-turbo car, so horsepower is limited to 135 ponies from the 5S-FE DOHC four. Fortunately, that engine is mated to a five-speed manual to make the most of that output. Even better, the seller says a new clutch was installed 46k miles ago, and the timing belt and water pump were refreshed just 26,000 miles back. New motor mounts, pads and rotors, and T-top seals are additional milestones in the car's service history.

This MR2 looks the part of a well-cared-for car, too. According to the seller, it was bought in Florida and spent much of its life in the South before being brought to New Jersey in 2018. When the present owner made that move, the car had 118,000 miles on the clock. It now has 136,788 miles, which averages about 2,400 miles a year under the current owner's care.

Overall, the car looks to be in great condition. The paint still pops, set off against factory alloys that show no evidence of injury. The engine looks cramped under its cover, and the sweeping buttresses make maintenance even more of a back-breaker, but at least it all looks intact.

The cabin doesn't appear cramped at all and looks quite handsome in its black-and-biscuit color scheme, with swanky leather upholstery on the seating surfaces. It all appears stock in here, save for a TRD-branded leather shift knob, although that does keep it in the family.

On the downside, the seller warns that the A/C compressor is grinding and hence they've removed the belt to keep it from turning and potentially doing more damage. The ad also makes no mention of the tires' age or condition. With so few miles driven each year, it's easy to let tires hang on longer than they should. The MR2 features a staggered setup, with larger, wider wheels in the back, meaning that rotating front to rear is out of the question, making the meats even more out of sight, out of mind.

On the plus side, the ad notes that all of the car's glass has been VIN-etched as an anti-theft measure. In addition, the car comes with a clean title, not one but two options for T-top storage, and three keys. Oddly, though the seller says this was a heavily optioned car, it does not seem to have a remote-entry key fob. Weird. There are also two manila folders full of maintenance records going back to the previous owner. Those will accompany the car in the sale.

On the face of it, this appears to be a solid example of a stock, mostly complete second-gen non-turbo MR2 with all the right specs and the promise of a well-managed service history. What's not to like, right? Well, there's that sweaty-Betty non-working A/C. That's going to cost a pretty penny to fix. We should also probably consider a new set of tires unless, upon inspection, they still seem to be in the game. Other than that, there don't seem to be any major red flags on this car. Plus, who doesn't dig an old MR2?

That only leaves us with the car's $14,000 asking price to either rejoice or bemoan. Let's talk about that. What's your opinion on this MR2 at that $14,000 asking? Does that sound fair given the car's presentation and specs? Or, at that price, is this Mister a miss?

#5761. CMS makes it official, codifying Medicare drug price negotiations established under IRA

CMS makes it official, codifying Medicare drug price negotiations established under IRA" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Against a backdrop of repeated industry challenges in court, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) is locking in the drug price negotiation framework established under the Biden-era Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

In turn, the process under which CMS selects certain high-spend Medicare Part B or Part D drugs and negotiates lower prices with manufacturers will carry on into 2029 and beyond. The rule codifies and expands policies previously established through guidance for the initial 2026-28 period.

The final rule is slated to go into effect Dec. 5, CMS said in a fact sheet accompanying Thursday’s announcement. By Feb. 1 of next year, CMS will select up to 20 drugs covered under Medicare Part B or Part D for price negotiations taking effect in 2029, with the potential to also select medicines included in previous rounds for renegotiation.

That upcoming group of drugs will make up the fourth cycle of pricing negotiations, with negotiated prices taking effect in 2029. CMS asserted that the rule gives both patients and drugmakers “a clear path forward as the agency builds on the program’s results and continues negotiating prices for high-cost drugs.”

The initial rounds of price negotiations have already included a slew of prominent brands, including Novo's semaglutide franchise of Wegovy and Ozempic and cancer meds like Bristol Myers Squibb’s Pomalyst, Pfizer’s Ibrance and AstraZeneca’s Calquence.

Meanwhile, the latest tranche of drugs selected earlier this year for negotiation, whose new prices would go into effect in 2028, includes notable entrants like Gilead’s HIV treatment Biktarvy, AbbVie’s Botox and Eli Lilly’s diabetes drug Trulicity, to name just a few.

Beyond codifying the framework for price negotiations in 2029 and subsequent years, CMS has also taken steps to fine-tune several elements of the program.

Namely, the rule finalizes a policy on how CMS classifies certain fixed-combination drugs, with the aim of addressing “potential program integrity concerns” that could encourage drugmakers to evade negotiated prices by steering patients toward new product formulations.

The rule also includes a provision establishing a temporary “small biotech floor” that prevents CMS from offering or accepting a counteroffer below a specified price floor for certain eligible small biotech drugs in 2029 and 2030. It also codifies two policies related to Medicare Part D intended to ensure plan coverage of medicines with a maximum fair price in effect and limit the prices plans pay pharmacies and other dispensing entities.

The IRA and the Medicare price negotiations it empowered have been frequent targets of the biopharma industry, which has broadly alleged that the policy is unconstitutional and that the pricing talks aren’t as voluntary as advertised. But attempts by major drugmakers and powerful trade organizations like the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) to push back on Medicare price negotiations have repeatedly stalled out.

In the interim, the U.S. government has made a separate and more recent push to rein in high prescription drug costs by leaning on President Donald Trump’s “most favored nation” (MFN) strategy.

“President Trump directed us to lower drug costs for Americans using every tool at our disposal,” CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., said in a statement announcing the new rule. “This rule provides additional tools to help CMS negotiate better deals, achieve greater savings for taxpayers and beneficiaries, and improve health outcomes for seniors who rely on the Medicare Prescription Drug Program.”

MFN, for its part, has yielded at times, controversial deals with more than two dozen drugmakers, generally involving commitments to price new medicines in line with prices in high-income comparator countries and offer MFN pricing on certain existing drugs through Medicaid.

Through those deals, which have also included investment commitments in the U.S., drugmakers have been able to secure temporary exemptions from the Trump administration’s threatened pharmaceutical import tariffs.

Around this week’s midterm elections, several Big Pharma executives have signaled that they expect little immediate change to their thinking around MFN. Nevertheless, the lack of transparency surrounding the deals has already drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers. With Democrats set to control both chambers of Congress beginning in January, the party may soon press harder to uncover the details of those agreements.

#5760. What Car Looks Best On Aftermarket Wheels?

Let's face it: Most stock wheels are, at best, fine. Occasionally one will stand out for its looks, usually because it's been made by Mercedes, but most OEM wheels are just some basic metal that you can wrap a tire around. That's good enough for getting from point A to point B, but we car enthusiasts often want better. Enter the entire world of aftermarket wheels, in any style you could dream up — rally turbofans, classic five-spokes, even teddy bears.

Today, though, we're not here to talk about the wheels themselves. We're here to talk about the cars they go on, and that brings us to a very broad question: What car looks best on aftermarket wheels? I'll accept answers to this in two forms, either cars that most need aftermarket wheels or cars that look best on the most different designs of aftermarket wheel. Are those criteria wide-open enough for you?

For both versions of the question, I think there's a single answer: The Toyobaru, most specifically the first-generation Scion FR-S/Subaru BRZ. It's a car that looks great on lightweight track wheels like Volk TE37s or Titan 7 T-S5s, but its style is just as well-suited to a set of bags and a BBS mesh design. Even a vintage wheel like the RS Watanabe, when scaled up to modern fitment, looks great on the Toyobaru chassis.

I think the car that looks best on aftermarket wheels is the first-generation Scion FR-S/Subaru BRZ, but what do you think? Do you think the Civic most needs a new set of shoes, or that the Lexus LS400 can do no wrong with any style of wheel face? Let me know in the comments below, and I'll collect my favorite answers later in the week. Bonus points if you've tried aftermarket wheels on a chassis yourself.

#5759. M1/M4 Agonist Relieved Schizophrenia Symptoms in Mid-Stage Trial

— Twice-daily dose hit primary and secondary endpoints

ML-007C-MA, an investigational muscarinic M1/M4 receptor agonist that combines betovumeline and fesoterodine fumarate, significantly improved schizophrenia symptoms in adults who had an acute exacerbation of psychosis, data from the randomized phase II ZEPHYR trial showed.

Those receiving a twice-daily ML-007C-MA dose of 210 mg betovumeline/3 mg fesoterodine fumarate (210/3 mg BID) achieved a statistically significant improvement in Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) total score compared with placebo at week 5 (least squares mean difference -4.5 points, P=0.015), reported Kimberly Thompson, PhD, of MapLight Therapeutics, and colleagues.

A once-daily dose of 330 mg betovumeline/6 mg fesoterodine, which delivered lower overall daily exposure, demonstrated numerical improvement over placebo on the primary endpoint but did not achieve statistical significance (-2.8 points, P=0.110).

The findings were presented at the Neuroscience Education Institute (NEI) Fall Congress in Colorado Springs, Colorado.

The 210/3 mg BID dose also met several other key secondary and prespecified endpoints at week 5:

Additionally, participants on the 210/3 mg BID regimen were 2.4 times more likely to achieve a ≥30% reduction in PANSS total score (P=0.021) and 2.8 times more likely to be deemed ready for discharge from an inpatient psychiatric setting by week 5 (P=0.002).

"Despite recent advances in schizophrenia treatment, patients and clinicians continue to need therapies that pair meaningful symptom control with a tolerability profile patients can sustain over time," co-author John Kane, MD, of the Donald and Barbara Zucker School of Medicine at Hofstra/Northwell in New York, said in a company statement.

"The ZEPHYR results are notable on both fronts: a statistically significant improvement on the primary endpoint and cognitive performance, alongside a meaningfully differentiated safety profile that matters most for the management of patients over time," he noted.

ML-007C-MA is an oral, extended-release, fixed-dose combination pairing the investigational M1/M4 agonist betovumeline (ML-007) with fesoterodine fumarate, a peripherally acting muscarinic antagonist. The co-formulation is engineered to sustain central M1/M4 activation in the brain while blocking peripheral cholinergic side effects like nausea, hypersalivation, and gastrointestinal (GI) distress.

By engaging muscarinic rather than dopamine receptors, this mechanism may offer an alternative pathway for patients who are refractory to or intolerant of traditional dopamine-blocking antipsychotics. Xanomeline and trospium chloride (Cobenfy) was the first M1/M4 receptor agonist approved in September 2024, establishing the first novel mechanistic class for schizophrenia in more than three decades.

The 25-site, double-blind trial enrolled 307 participants ages 18 to 64 years with a schizophrenia diagnosis confirmed by the Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview. Eligibility criteria required a baseline PANSS total score between 80 and 120, a score of 4 or higher on two or more positive symptom items, a CGI-S score of 4 or higher, and no concurrent antipsychotic therapy.

In the 210/3 mg BID arm, the mean age was 42 years, 70% were male, and 74% identified as Black. Disease severity at baseline was high, reflected by a mean PANSS total score of 96 (on a scale of 30 to 210) and a mean CGI-S score of 5 (on a scale of 1 to 7).

ML-007C-MA was generally well tolerated, with the majority of treatment-emergent adverse events categorized as mild or moderate. No serious or drug-related severe adverse events occurred, and investigators noted an absence of urinary retention, metabolic dysregulation, hepatic liability, or extrapyramidal movement-related signals.

Approximately 7% of participants discontinued treatment due to adverse events (2% attributable to GI issues) compared with 1% in the placebo group.

"No fasting requirement and a one-dose titration support a tolerability profile that is expected to translate into real-world adherence," the researchers noted.

MapLight announced plans to meet with the FDA to discuss phase III trial designs.

#5758. Hims & Hers inks deal with Eli Lilly to offer branded weight loss drugs

Hims & Hers inks deal with Eli Lilly to offer branded weight loss drugs" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hims & Hers struck a deal with Eli Lilly to offer the drugmaker’s branded obesity treatments through its online health and wellness platform.

Under the agreement, Eli Lilly will give Hims & Hers pharmacies direct access to its U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved GLP-1 medications at self-pay prices. Eligible patients on the Hims & Hers platform can be prescribed and order Eli Lilly's injectable Zepbound (tirzepatide) and daily oral medication Foundayo (orforglipron) without leaving the company's platform.

Prior to this agreement, Lilly drugs were available to patients on Hims & Hers only if they left the site and went to Lilly's direct-to-consumer platform, LillyDirect.

Shares of Hims & Hers jumped 8% Friday following news of the Eli Lilly partnership.

The agreement brings together Lilly’s obesity medicines and Hims & Hers’ consumer platform to expand consumers' access to FDA-approved weight loss drugs, the companies said.

"Patients can complete a consultation, receive a prescription if their provider determines it is appropriate and have an FDA-approved Lilly medicine shipped directly to their home, all in one seamless experience," the companies said in a press release.

Self-pay pricing starts at $149 per month for Foundayo and $299 per month for Zepbound.

"At Lilly, we are always looking for new ways to help more people get the medicines they need, and that means meeting patients where they already are," said Ilya Yuffa, executive vice president and president, Lilly USA and global customer capabilities, Eli Lilly and Company, in a statement. "Millions of people turn to Hims & Hers for their care, and through this agreement, those patients now have a simple, more direct way to get FDA-approved Lilly medicine at an affordable price if prescribed."

Hims & Hers' technology platform supports provider outreach, follow-up care and treatment planning. Weight loss patients on Hims & Hers receive a membership experience that includes 24/7 access to a care team, nutrition guidance, regular clinical check-ins and access to the Hims & Hers Weight Loss community, according to the company.

The agreement with Eli Lilly mirrors Hims & Hers' partnership with Novo Nordisk, which has been selling its branded weight loss drugs Wegovy and Ozempic through Hims & Hers since March. Novo had previously sued the telehealth company for offering compounded versions of its medications. Hims & Hers' agreement with Novo marked a shift in its obesity strategy toward FDA-approved branded GLP-1 treatments and away from cheaper compounded GLP-1 drugs.

Earlier this year, Hims & Hers took heat from the pharmaceutical manufacturer and federal regulators after announcing plans to launch a knockoff of Novo's oral pill. It backed down from those plans under pressure.

Hims & Hers stated that it never offered access to compounded copies of Lilly’s GLP-1 drugs and has committed not to do so in the future.

As part of the agreement, the companies have committed to protecting independent clinical decision-making, so that providers on the Hims & Hers platform continue to prescribe the treatment they determine is right for each patient.

“Lilly is one of the most innovative pharmaceutical companies in history, and I’m incredibly proud that Hims & Hers is a part of making sure more people can access the medicines they’ve created,” said Andrew Dudum, co-founder and CEO of Hims & Hers, in a statement. “By working together, we’re not just reaching more people with obesity with seamless, personal access to FDA-approved Lilly medicine. We’re showing the industry what innovators can achieve for customers everywhere when we work together to make the world well.”

Hims & Hers has faced financial pressure as it shifts from high-margin compounded GLP-1s to lower-margin branded weight-loss drugs. The company posted a $92 million loss in Q1, including $33 million in restructuring costs, largely from write-downs of its compounded GLP-1 supply chain, which executives said faced “risk of obsolescence.”

In Q2, Hims & Hers reported an $86 million loss, compared with a $43 million profit a year earlier. The quarter included $81 million in one-time costs, including expenses tied to its exit from compounded GLP-1s.
