#5641. Exclusive: FormAssembly overhauls its platform to expand into AI-powered process automation

FormAssembly Inc., a provider of online data collection and workflow automation software, today announced a complete platform overhaul that expands its capabilities beyond building forms to automating complex business processes using artificial intelligence.

The new platform, which the company said took seven months to develop, combines form creation, workflow automation, integrations and compliance management in a single no-code environment.

It also introduces conversational AI agents that can collect information through natural language interactions and support for the Model Context Protocol, enabling external AI agents to interact with FormAssembly’s software.

The launch marks a significant expansion for the 20-year-old company, which has traditionally focused on helping organizations collect structured information securely and integrate it into business applications. “We’re about how people share information with organizations and what happens after that,” said founder and Chief Executive Cedric Savarese.

The new platform builds on the AI assistant FormAssembly introduced last October, which enabled users to generate forms and configure workflows using natural language instructions. The latest release extends those capabilities to entire business processes, including approvals, document generation, electronic signatures and payments.

For example, a municipal government could describe an application process for obtaining a permit to hold an event in a public park. The platform’s assistant, called Fai, could then generate the necessary forms, approval workflows and documentation requirements.

“You can explain what you need in plain English to your agent, and the agent will build the entire process in a couple of minutes,” Savarese said.

FormAssembly claims the AI-assisted builder can reduce development time from days or weeks to minutes. Savarese said the company based those estimates on recreating existing customer workflows using the new platform.

A second major addition is conversational intake agents that replace traditional forms with interactive voice or text conversations. The agents use predefined data structures to guide conversations, answer questions and convert unstructured responses into information suitable for downstream systems.

The agents can also personalize interactions using previously collected information, although Savarese emphasized that access to that information is restricted by default.

FormAssembly uses frontier AI models, primarily from Anthropic PBC, rather than developing its own. Savarese said the company has zero-retention agreements with Anthropic and OpenAI Group PBC to protect customer information.

The revamped platform also adds governance capabilities that evaluate workflows against predefined compliance policies before publication. Organizations can use built-in rules or define their own requirements based on internal policies and applicable regulations. Potential violations are flagged for human review rather than automatically blocked.

MCP support and application programming interfaces enable customers to create and manage FormAssembly workflows through external systems without accessing the software’s traditional interface.

Savarese said this approach could protect established software companies from the risk that AI agents will make conventional software-as-a-service applications obsolete.

“People will use AI agents, but they use AI agents to drive software, not to replace it,” he said.

The company isn’t positioning itself as a comprehensive competitor to business process management vendors such as ServiceNow Inc. Instead, it intends to concentrate on processes that begin with collecting information from people.

Existing customers won’t be forced to migrate immediately. Savarese said migrations aren’t planned until January, and pricing for existing customers remains uncertain. More sophisticated automation capabilities could carry additional charges depending on customers’ current subscriptions.

FormAssembly, founded in 2006, raised its first outside funding of $10 million in 2019 after 13 years of bootstrapping. The company says it has thousands of customers, particularly in regulated industries such as healthcare, financial services, education and government.

#5639. David Muir Shares Rare Look at Personal Life Ahead of His Birthday—Inside His $7 Million Lakeside Estate in Upstate New York

When it comes to his personal life, famed journalist David Muir tends to keep quiet, but the “World News Tonight” anchor recently pulled back the curtain just before his 53rd birthday.

In a Nov. 7 Instagram post, the ABC News anchor shared a wholesome update—a snap of his German short-haired pointer, Axel, as the pair set out to enjoy the fall foliage.

Although Muir let the photo speak for itself—offering nothing more than an autumnal leaf emoji as the caption—he occasionally uploads content of Axel, usually to show off their outdoor adventures.

In a 2025 interview with People magazine, the broadcaster shared some rare insight into his home life, noting that while he’s based in Manhattan for work, he enjoys retreating to a spot just outside his hometown of Syracuse.

“I’d say my most comfortable element is being outside, covered in mud,” he told the publication, adding that he had recently taken a trip to his property in upstate New York, enjoying the surroundings despite the fact that it had been “pouring rain.”

In 2019, Muir purchased a $7 million property on Skaneateles Lake—a small town about a 30-minute drive from Syracuse.

“This job takes me all over the world, and I can’t think of a better place to catch my breath,” he told Syracuse.com at the time.

The 4,300-square-foot abode is a single-family home set on a 6-acre plot of land with water access. The six-bedroom, 2.5-bathroom dwelling was built in 1890 and seems to be the perfect place to escape from the bustle of the city—or a job as demanding as Muir’s.

“When you’re out there on the lake, smelling the same air that you smelled when you were on your BMX bike back when you were a kid, there’s something really fueling about that and connected about it,” he told People magazine in 2025. “You just feel like you’re home again.”

Over the years, Muir has invited his Instagram followers to enjoy the dazzling lake views he enjoys during his weekends away.

In a 2020 post, he remarked, “I love being home,” in a caption of a photo of himself cracking a smile while enjoying a boat ride across the lake.

A few distinct features of Muir’s historic home have taken up real estate on his Instagram profile, as well, including the charming wraparound porch that hugs the Skaneateles Lake property, which made an appearance in a 2022 post he shared for his sister’s birthday, where he made a note to give a shoutout to “porches.”

He purchased the 2,280-square-foot abode for $4.2 million in 2013, the same year he became the host of “World News Tonight,” following in Diane Sawyer’s footsteps.

Located on West Fourth Street, the three-bedroom, three-bathroom structure was built in 1877 by Alexander M. McKean, and Muir put it on the market for $7.5 million in April 2025.

“Inside, the original details of this 15 foot wide house have been lovingly restored,” the listing explained. “The renovation maintains and respects the character of this remarkable home, while bringing it completely up-to-date, upgrading electricity, plumbing, and gas service but keeping and restoring original details including hardware, flooring, fixtures, and historic plaster medallions and moldings throughout.”

Perhaps the most stunning feature of the townhouse was the primary bedroom, which spanned the entire fourth level of the building. With a bed area that faced over quiet gardens and a full wall of closets, the suite also included a spacious office and a windowed bathroom with a vintage claw-foot tub.

The home lingered on the market for a few weeks before it was removed and relisted, but nearly six months later, it was sold for $6.85 million.

#5638. AWS commits $100M in AI and cloud credits to health groups in underserved communities

Amazon Web Services Inc. today committed $100 million worth of artificial intelligence and cloud technology over five years to health organizations working in underserved communities around the world, provided to recipients as AWS credits.

The new AWS Health Impact Initiative is taking aim at a cost problem that AWS says is keeping many of those organizations out of the current wave of AI adoption. AWS points to survey data to explain the focus on credits.

An independent survey of 83 of the more than 400 organizations supported under the company’s earlier AWS Health Equity Initiative found that 60% saw cost as the main barrier to cloud adoption where they operate. Most ranked AWS credits as their highest-priority need. That program began in 2021 with $40 million behind it, and the total had grown to $60 million by the time the last of it was handed out in July 2024.

Timing matters too. A World Economic Forum forecast cited by AWS has generative AI use climbing faster in health care than in any other field. If the organizations closest to underserved patients fall behind on adopting it, AWS argues, health gaps will widen.

Agents and AI are reshaping health services, said Dr. Rowland Illing, chief medical officer and director of health care and life sciences at AWS, and they “too often don’t reach the communities that need them most.” Illing framed the initiative as an extension of the company’s stated aim of democratizing AI and cloud-based health technology.

Any area of health care is eligible, and AWS has singled out three for added weight. The first is access to health services, where AWS wants to support diagnostic testing and stronger health infrastructure in places such as rural areas and low- and middle-income countries.

A second area covers research into women’s and children’s health, with better data and more inclusive studies as the goal. Women’s health draws just 5% of health research funding, the company said, and as many as half the medicines given to children lack pediatric clinical validation.

Healthy food is the third area. AWS said malnutrition among pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers and adolescent girls has climbed 25% since 2020 in the 12 countries hit hardest by the global food and nutrition crisis. Projects there could improve food distribution or predict food security patterns.

Recipients AWS highlighted include women’s health data nonprofit Eve’s Ark, which collects research datasets that are at risk of disappearing when a lab closes or a grant ends. Co-founder and Chief Executive Melissa Antal Iftimie said the group started with a small AWS award and “a single at-risk dataset.” The archive now holds more than a petabyte of women’s health data on AWS, and the group is building a secure research environment where scientists can work with it.

In Haiti, primary care provider Care 2 Communities runs a network of community clinics that has served 350,000 people and handles almost 120,000 patient visits a year. Its electronic medical records sit on AWS, which brings centralized, real-time data to clinics in rural parts of the country. School meals for more than 2.35 million children in India come out of kitchens run by the Akshaya Patra Foundation every school day, and the foundation uses AWS to run those kitchens and get meals out to schools.

Eligibility runs well past health charities to government agencies, research institutions and companies, and AWS will consider a project at any stage up to full production.

Organizations with an AWS account team can submit proposals through it, and a public portal is open to everyone else. Each application has to estimate how many lives the project will improve, and AWS goes through submissions every week. Successful applicants receive credits sized to their own AWS Pricing Calculator estimate of what a project needs, or a starting allocation of up to $10,000. Awardees have 12 months to use the credits and can ask to have that window stretched to 24.

#5637. Casino Mogul Steve Wynn Sells His $70 Million Central Park Condo as Manhattan Luxury Market Heats Up

Casino billionaire Steve Wynn has finally unloaded his Central Park duplex penthouse, making it the top luxury sale of a record-breaking week in Manhattan.

The mogul's prewar condo at 50 Central Park South—first listed in 2022 for $90 million, the most expensive in the country at the time—eventually saw its price drop to $70 million.

Even at this steep discount, it still took two years for the condo to find a taker. The duplex went into contract last week with Serena Boardman of Sotheby's International Realty as the listing agent (co-exclusive with Deborah Grubman of Corcoran).

The sale means the casino magnate failed to turn a profit on the 10,875-square-foot condo. But given that, according to Forbes, Wynn is worth $4.3 billion, he likely isn't sweating it too much.

The Billionaires Row duplex takes up the 30th and 31st floors within the 36-story Ritz-Carlton Residences, formerly the Hotel St. Moritz, which opened in 1930. The top 12 floors are the private homes.

The penthouse, formerly owned by real estate developer Christopher M. Jeffries, comes with an esteemed pedigree.

It was Jeffries' Millennium Partners that purchased the Emory Roth–designed building in 1999 and reimagined it along with the Ritz-Carlton Hotel Co. Jeffries was once married to Princess Yasmin Aga Khan, the only child of Prince Aly Khan and movie legend Rita Hayworth.

Yet the real selling point of the duplex is its sweeping Central Park views. With floors that aren't too high, from the vantage of the 45-foot long terrace, it feels as if one is sitting in the famed park's trees—a "bird's-eye perspective," as the listing puts it. Another terrace along the western wall stretches 28 feet.

With three bedrooms, four full baths, and two half-baths, the prewar unit features 10 grandly arched windows, a marble staircase, 15-foot coffered ceilings, and a living room that used to be the St. Moritz ballroom.

Modern touches include a chef's kitchen; a breakfast room with its own terrace; a primary bedroom with Central Park views, en suite bathroom, gym, and dressing room; a staff room with laundry; and a library.

As the condo sits atop the flagship Ritz-Carlton hotel, it comes with access to the amenities of the global luxury name, including the La Prairie spa and health club, a business center, the Contour Bar and Lounge, in-room dining services, and housekeeping services.

The unit has $31,362 in monthly dues on top of $15,500 in taxes.

As for why a property offering such grandeur may have taken so long to move, luxury broker Michael Reisor with Compass-affiliated Reisor.Team, who is familiar with the building, says, "Properties like this are wonderful but specific. There's a more limited buyer pool."

Despite the park views and architectural significance, it's still a century-old building, and buyers at this price range have their pick.

However, "when buyers at this level want prewar charm and detail, there is only one way to get it authentically, and that is to buy of that era," he says. "Are there people in droves wanting to pay at this level for prewar? No, but there are people who do. It's usually a more sophisticated buyer.

"They want that, 'This is classic New York.'"

The final price isn't yet known, but Reisor says, "We can assume it was right around [the ask price], if not right on."

The buyer hasn't been revealed, and listing agent Boardman did not return a call for comment.

One unique aspect of the 50 Central Park prewar is that it is a condo, not a co-op. Prewar buildings—built between the late 1880s and 1939—are typically co-ops.

In general, condos outsell co-ops each week—and after two weeks of the gap between them being slim, for the week ending Nov. 8, condos were far ahead, 34 contracts versus 7. Co-ops tend to be cheaper, with an average ask of $8.6 million last week versus $10.5 million for condos, according to Olshan Realty.

Another unusual feature of the sprawling duplex is that it has only three bedrooms. Often condos at this scale have expanded to four or more. Last week's top sale, a $31 million penthouse condo at 111 Murray St. in Tribeca, had five bedrooms.

"It's more of a psychological sticking point than an actual need," Reisor says of a high-end buyer's desire for plentiful bedrooms. "They think, 'At a certain price, I should be overflowing with bedrooms.' Even if they never need them."

Whoever snapped up the trophy unit likely wanted to be in that particular building, which is low-density, has only 11 private residences inside of a global luxury brand, and comes with a glamorous history and illustrious architect.

"It could be someone high-profile," Reisor speculates of the mystery buyer. "Someone high-profile would want something like this."

The Wynn sale was one of a slew of high-end contracts last week, with 45 signed, a big leap of 11 over the week before, and the biggest luxury sales week for the entire year. Of that, an astonishing 14 sales were priced over $10 million.

The New York City pied-à-terre tax doesn't seem to be squeezing the top end of the market. Reisor says last week's surge of luxury (over $4 million) buys can be attributed to the midterm elections.

"We always see a freeze-up before elections," he says. "The enemy to any financial market, including the housing market, is uncertainty. The biggest thing in play is that the election happened; it's over."

Additionally, he thinks that the "blue wave" was a positive for the high-end market, speculating that President Donald Trump's somewhat chastened stance on immigration is good news for monied buyers.

"This is especially relevant to New York City because of international buyers," he says, theorizing that affluent foreign buyers are wondering, "Will this be more friendly to me as an international purchaser?"

The second-highest contract of the week was a triplex penthouse with an asking price of $25.36 million. The condo, EA at 95 Madison Ave., is also in a 1912 prewar building. Although smaller at 8,355 square feet, the condo came with six bedrooms.

Formerly the Emmet Building, the Flatiron building is a quick stroll to Madison Square Park. Its Gothic facade is made from limestone and marble, reflecting the "architectural Golden Age," says the listing, which was held by Vicki Zhi Saali of Global Real Estate Ventures Group.

#5636. Only a Quarter of U.S. Households Have Children at Home

Household composition is a fundamental driver of housing demand, influencing everything from floor plans and bedroom counts to community amenities and long-term land strategies. Understanding how household composition is changing can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to serve different types of buyers.

As of 2024, 25.4% of U.S. households had children under age 18 living at home, according to Zonda’s analysis of U.S. Census data. Put another way, nearly three out of every four households did not have children at home.

The finding is consistent with trends visible among home buyers: the 2025 Home Buyers and Sellers Generational Trends Report from NAR showed that only 24% of buyers had children under 18, a historic low.

Several structural demographic forces help explain this shift, including fertility rates below replacement levels, later family formation, and an aging population that has contributed to more empty nesters, retirees, and older adults living independently. At the same time, households without children, including DINKS (dual income, no kids), represent an important part of housing demand.

These shifts highlight the changing composition of household types shaping housing demand and reinforce the importance of segmentation over assumptions. The traditional family household remains an important customer, but understanding the needs of other household types can help inform product planning and identify opportunities to reach a broader range of buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

#5635. Joanna Gaines Says an ‘Upset’ Buyer Lost Interest in Magnolia’s $7 Million Mansion Renovation Because She Preferred the ‘Before’ Photos

Joanna Gaines has had a successful career, thanks to her signature design aesthetic, but a recent real estate snafu served as a brutal reminder that not everyone has the same taste.

During an appearance on Kylie Kelce’s podcast, “Not Gonna Lie,” the “Fixer Upper” star revealed that her most involved renovation yet lost a buyer who much preferred the “before” photos.

Joanna and her husband, Chip Gaines, recently tackled the transformation of a 15,000-square-foot mansion in their hometown of Waco, TX. The process was documented in the upcoming Magnolia Network show “Fixer Upper: Chip Bought a Mansion,” and it appears the project was quite the struggle.

While the Gaineses are a solid team, Chip actually purchased the sprawling estate without Joanna, a decision she called a “bold move.” Although the mom of five vouched the property would “never be a fixer,” she changed her mind after the property lingered on the market without much interest for more than three years.

The 1990s-built palace is in an incredible location, set on a 5.7-acre lot boasting striking views of Lake Waco. But the outdated ‘90s interiors needed a serious face-lift, and when Chip and Joanna set out to work their magic on the abode, they realized it needed more work than they had anticipated.

The process was grueling, but to add insult to injury, an interaction with an interested buyer made it seem like it was all for nothing.

“If you look online, the pictures you see is of the ‘before,’” Joanna said. The listing, held by Amanda Nesbitt of Magnolia Realty, keeps the “after” images a secret to avoid spoiling the show.

In a twist of fate, the prospective buyer had fallen in love with the outdated photos in the listing and was disappointed to learn that Chip and Joanna had stripped the home of its former McMansion glory.

Joanna recalled that on “the day of the reveal,” the real estate agents called to let the Gaineses know that a “qualified buyer” had “fallen in love” with the estate and wanted to put an offer in. The HGTV personality offered to give the buyer a walk through the home to chat about the changes they had made, only to realize that the renovation was a deal breaker.

“She said, ‘Well, what did they do?’ She was like, ‘I liked the pictures that I saw,’” Joanna said.

Unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to retain the buyer, who decided not to come for the viewing at all.

“The lady was so upset,” Joanna recalled. “She was like, ‘I don’t understand why she removed all the red and gold.’”

“It’s like, Chip was right,” she continued. “He could have sold this thing as is. We didn’t have to touch it. I’m like, ‘This is a joke.' I finally did it. I revealed it, and now we have a buyer and she’s upset that I fixed it up.”

The six-bedroom, 11-bathroom mansion is still on the market, asking $7.39 million. Although the new furnishings are still under wraps, viewers can get a look when the series premieres on Dec. 27 on Magnolia Network and HGTV.

The missed opportunity wasn’t the only revelation Joanna shared on the podcast episode. She also divulged that lately, she and Chip have been discussing expanding the family.

“When I had Crew at 40, I said, ‘Chip, I want him to have more siblings,’” she said. “I really thought I’d have nine children. I’m that lady. Look at my hair. Don’t I look like a lady that would have nine kids? And he was not open to it. Guess who’s open to it now? At 48?”

Joanna went on to share that her husband is “telling everyone” that she’s pregnant, even though she is not. From their adult children to a crowd of 2,000 people at a recent speaking engagement, Chip has continued to share the false news in an attempt to “speak it out into the universe.”

“So that whole audience thinks I’m pregnant. I don’t know what’s happening, but I’m not,” she confirmed.

#5633. Diagrid’s Dapr 1.19 lightens AI agent workflows and drops a control-plane service

Agent infrastructure startup Diagrid Inc. today released Dapr 1.19 with changes that cut the overhead of the durable workflows behind long-running artificial intelligence agents.

Operators of the open-source runtime can also drop one of its control-plane services. Until 1.19, Dapr’s workflow engine shipped the entire execution history to the worker on every step.

Each one adds to that history. On a job that runs for hours or fans out into dozens of parallel tasks, the payload keeps growing, and Diagrid said that pushed up latency and memory use. Now a worker keeps what it already holds and gets only new events.

That makes the data sent per step independent of how long a workflow has been running. Workers still replay the full history locally. The smaller transfers go only to workers that advertise support for them, which in 1.19 means those built on Dapr’s Java and Python software development kits.

Mark Fussell, Diagrid’s co-founder and chief product officer, said an agent “that runs all afternoon and splits into 50 tasks can’t haul its entire history across the network on every step.”

A second workflow change, an opt-in preview feature called WorkflowsFastPath, stops pushing every workflow event through a durable scheduler reminder. Wake-ups and local activities are handled in place. The reminder path stays as a backstop for recovery, and in Diagrid’s engine benchmarks median step latency fell from 553 milliseconds to 153 milliseconds with the feature on.

Two services have made up Dapr’s control plane until now, and a new mode in 1.19 retires Placement, which distributes the actor placement table. The surviving Scheduler service handles jobs, reminders and workflow scheduling, and it already tracks cluster membership and pushes state to sidecars the same way Placement does.

Yaron Schneider, a co-creator of Dapr who is also Diagrid’s co-founder and chief technology officer, said the pair “matured as two services doing overlapping work.” With the mode on, the Scheduler takes over actor placement and the standalone Placement service is no longer deployed. That spares operators a stateful service and the Raft consensus cluster behind it. Reminders get faster too, because the Scheduler knows which sidecar owns each actor.

Scaling events are also less disruptive. A host joining or leaving used to pause placement across the entire namespace while Dapr re-sent its placement table. In the new mode, only the affected actor types are locked and updated, and the rest keep serving traffic.

New alpha building blocks in 1.19 are aimed at developers of AI applications. A Vector building block offers a portable application programming interface for storing and querying embeddings through similarity search, with Meilisearch as its first supported component.

Binary Store streams large files such as model outputs in chunks so they never have to sit in memory whole. Its first components cover Amazon S3 and the object stores from Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle.

Developers working in .NET get Actors.Next, a new actor SDK that generates proxies and registration code at compile time, which cuts runtime overhead and lets actor apps compile with Native AOT.

Dapr 1.19 is available now. WorkflowsFastPath ships turned off, and the Scheduler placement mode is enabled through a Helm setting once every sidecar runs 1.19, with no sidecar restart needed to switch it on or off. Teams running Dapr on Kubernetes can manage the upgrade through Diagrid’s Dapr Ops Dashboard, and the company said the tool typically supports new releases within 24 hours.

#5632. New NAR Policies Allow MLS Data-Feed Restrictions, Photo Copyright

In the face of a rapid and accelerating shift in the MLS landscape, the National Association of Realtors® (NAR) announced today that it is introducing two new optional MLS policies, focused on topics at the forefront of the ongoing debate—namely, data and membership—along with tweaks to MLS committee eligibility and a new policy statement.

According to a release from NAR, MLSs will be allowed “at their discretion” to copyright photos and property descriptions submitted by members, and restrict the use of data feeds based on criteria that are “reasonable, objective and applied equally to all participants.”

“These updates reflect our commitment to ensuring MLS policies remain relevant, effective and responsive to the needs of today’s real estate industry,” said NAR CEO Nykia Wright in a statement.

The changes—approved by the Multiple Listing Issues and Policies Committee during NAR’s annual meetings in New Orleans—come at a time when MLSs are scrambling to keep up with demands from brokers and evolving technology. Many MLSs—both Realtor®- and broker-owned—have announced national platforms, and proactively shifted their policies around listing syndication and data.

Cameron Paine, CEO of MARIS MLS, tells RISMedia via email that “MLSs can only benefit from adoption of sensible improvements to protect their data.”

“(T)he new NAR rules are positive efforts toward that end,” he adds.

The new policy statement, also focused on data, “reinforces” that “the use of MLS data must comply with applicable MLS participation or data licensing agreements and be connected to providing real estate brokerage services, preparing appraisals, or other valuations of real property.”

An NAR spokesperson clarified that MLSs can still license data for other purposes—for example, to tech companies or universities—but that this must be at the discretion of the MLS. Enforcement also remains a “local discretion” matter, the spokesperson said.

Asked if the new data feed policy could be used to restrict MLS data feeds based on broad criteria—for instance, where a participant is located geographically—the NAR spokesperson said that the use of “(l)ocal eligibility requirements will be matters of local discretion…subject to those requirements being reasonable, objective, and equally applied to all participants, and applicable laws.”

Notably, Chicago-based MRED (not affiliated with NAR) made waves in the spring by briefly cutting Zillow off from its listing feed, claiming the portal violated a different rule when it banned certain limited-marketed listings. Compass had pressured several other MLSs—unsuccessfully—to cut Zillow’s feed based on that same rule.

Compass has also been outspoken about the alleged misuse of data by MLSs, specifically by recruiting companies, and is embroiled in lawsuits with a handful of big MLSs, mostly focused on policies restricting off-MLS marketing.

The policy allowing MLSs to copyright photos and listing descriptions comes as MLSs face AI aggregation and scrapers, with at least one big MLS directly confronting AI companies that were pilfering data—including listing descriptions and photos. NAR clarified that brokers “retain the right to independently use and license their own listing content,” and can opt-out of “assigning a copyright interest to the MLS.”

“Organized real estate, including banks and lenders, depend on the MLS to provide timely, accurate and comprehensive data, but the MLS has been consistently undermined by the wholesale theft and unfettered scraping of MLS compilation data,” Paine said.

Paine also characterized the new rules as “overdue,” adding that “any efforts to improve the qualifications of those serving on the MLS Committee are welcome.”

Jesse Williams is content director for RISMedia Premier.

#5630. Broadcom open-sources its Kubernetes VM manager

Broadcom Inc. is contributing an open-source project for managing virtual machines with Kubernetes to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, part of an effort to simplify operations across increasingly diverse enterprise computing environments.

The company announced today that its VM application programming interface project has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox, the entry point for early-stage cloud-native projects. VM API  provides a vendor-neutral framework for provisioning and managing virtual machines using the same APIs that Kubernetes employs to orchestrate modular and portable software containers.

Broadcom also announced an initiative to standardize application behavior across Kubernetes distributions and expanded support for third-party software on VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service.

The announcements, made at KubeCon North America in Salt Lake City, reflect the growing need for infrastructure that can support traditional applications alongside modern containerized and artificial intelligence workloads.

Although Kubernetes has become the dominant platform for container orchestration, virtual machines remain central to enterprise computing. A Linux Foundation survey of 492 practitioners scheduled to be released today found that VMs account for 53% of production applications, with most respondents expecting that proportion to remain stable. Among organizations expanding their VM deployments, 34% cited AI and agentic workloads as contributing factors.

Broadcom’s VM API project addresses the operational complexity of managing VMs and containers separately. It uses Kubernetes’ declarative management model to create and manage virtual machines across different infrastructure providers while preserving capabilities such as hardware isolation and specialized input/output performance.

“We want to do the same thing now for virtual machines,” said Prashanth Shenoy, Broadcom’s chief marketing officer and vice president of marketing for cloud platform, infrastructure and solutions, referring to Kubernetes’ existing Cluster API initiative.

The goal is to provide consistent management across environments without requiring organizations to abandon their existing virtualization investments.

“Ultimately, our goal is to make virtual machines first-class citizens of a Kubernetes environment without sacrificing what makes them distinct and valuable for our customers,” Shenoy said.

The project could also simplify operations for administrators accustomed to working with Kubernetes rather than maintaining separate management tools for virtualized and containerized infrastructure.

Broadcom’s second initiative addresses a different interoperability problem: inconsistent application behavior across Kubernetes distributions.

The company is co-chairing a newly established Workload Conformance Working Group to develop common expectations for how applications operate across Kubernetes environments.

Existing conformance programs verify that Kubernetes distributions support standard APIs, but that doesn’t guarantee applications will behave identically across platforms. Differences in infrastructure capabilities, configuration and operational practices can introduce incompatibilities.

“Just because two Kubernetes environments are conformant doesn’t necessarily mean that the application will behave consistently across both,” Shenoy said.

The proposed workload conformance standard would help software vendors reduce the need to certify applications separately for individual Kubernetes distributions while giving enterprises greater confidence in application portability.

Broadcom also announced more than 20 newly validated partner solutions for VKS, the Kubernetes runtime integrated into VMware Cloud Foundation.

The validations span observability, security, data management, AI, application delivery, networking and storage. They are intended to help organizations deploy Kubernetes workloads using familiar third-party tools without requiring extensive integration or changes to existing operational practices.

Broadcom said its broader VKS ecosystem now includes more than 90 independent software vendors participating in testing and validation.

Dean Norris is looking for a buyer for his 11-acre Temecula, CA, estate, listing the hilltop property for $3,199,000—after his wife, Bridget Norris, filed for divorce.

The “Breaking Bad” actor is bidding farewell to the property he and his estranged wife bought for $1.7 million in 2024.

According to Page Six, the property first came on the market in September, roughly a year and a half after Bridget filed for divorce in Riverside County.

The property, which is listed with Sherrie Snyder of Allison James Estates & Homes, is described as a "timeless architecturally designed estate with explosive commanding views from one of the most desirable area's of De Luz."

The palatial compound sits on 11.37 acres and totals 7,315 square feet of living space across the main residence and guesthouse.

Together, the two homes have nine bedrooms, seven full bathrooms, and two half-bathrooms. The current asking price is about $1.47 million above what the couple paid.

At roughly 6,067 square feet, the main house contains seven of the estate’s nine bedrooms, with six on the first floor.

Both the living room and the family room boast cozy fireplaces. A third fireplace is in the primary suite, which features exposed ceiling beams and a walk-in closet.

"At the heart of the home, the spectacular family room offers an impressive setting appointed with a fireplace & custom built-ins," reads the listing.

#5628. Significant Pent-Up Demand Could Be Released If Supply, Affordability and Confidence Improve

A wave of sidelined homebuyers could be poised to flood the housing market if a trifecta of housing supply and affordability improve and consumer confidence picks up. How likely that is remains unclear, however.

That was the theme of a market outlook delivered this past Friday by National Association of Realtors® Chief Economist Lawrence Yun at the Residential Economic Issues and Trends Forum at NAR NXT in New Orleans.

According to a release, Yun compared today’s economy with the year 2000, noting since then, the U.S. population has grown from 281 million to 350 million, and payroll jobs have risen from 132 million to 159 million. He said housing wealth has grown from $7 trillion to $35 trillion, yet existing-home sales are running near 4 million this year, below the 5.2 million homes sold in 2000.

“Affordability is tough, but people’s incomes are rising, and if somehow mortgage rates go down, think about the potential housing demand that could be released to the marketplace,” Yun said.

On supply, Yun noted that inventory has risen as sales have slowed. Months’ supply is at its highest level since 2015, and the median home took 33 days to go from listing to contract in September.

“Homes are staying on the market a little longer than before,” Yun said. “With longer days on market, you have to be realistic to the market condition. Otherwise, buyers will reject the homes on the market.”

Yun said a rebound in consumer confidence would also be key. Consumer sentiment has fallen to roughly half its 2000 level and is now worse than during the Great Recession, even as the economy has added jobs, he said.

“If we can boost confidence levels, maybe that can also change the dynamics,” Yun said.

Jessica Lautz, NAR deputy chief economist and vice president of research, presented highlights from the newly released 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. First-time buyers made up 22% of all buyers, near the historic low, and the median age of first-time buyers held at a record-high 40.

“First-time home buyers are struggling,” Lautz said. “They’re not struggling just with housing affordability. They’re also struggling with rent. They’re struggling with student loan debt, and a rising issue for first-time home buyers is childcare costs.”

Sellers stayed in their homes for a median of 12 years before selling, the longest on record.

“The golden handcuffs of low interest rate mortgages is true. People are holding on to those properties for longer periods of time,” said Lautz. “It’s why we need to build more housing inventory—especially affordable housing inventory—for the potential first-time home buyers who are out there.”

Use of real estate professionals remained strong: 90% of buyers purchased through an agent, the highest share in four decades, and a record 92% of sellers used an agent.

“Sellers want agents to price that home competitively, find that qualified buyer, help with marketing, and make sure they get to the closing table in a time frame that they need to do so,” Lautz said.

Routine maintenance, sensible storage, suitable flood protection and a clear emergency plan can help homeowners prepare more effectively. The right approach depends on the property, its surroundings and the conditions it may face. Read more.

#5627. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5625. These Sun Belt States Are Falling Behind on Home Permitting, Study Finds

In an era of strained housing affordability, new-home construction is one of the keys to easing the housing shortage. And some states are building faster than others.

South Carolina, Idaho, and North Carolina lead the nation in permitting new homes, according to data from the Lied Center for Real Estate at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. On the other hand, the more affordable Midwest was stagnant. UNLV looked at data from the U.S. Census Bureau in the first eight months of this year compared to 2025.

Meanwhile, in the Sun Belt, which has been a bright spot in housing production the past few years, some states are falling behind, a new study finds. UNLV found slowing permitting activity in Texas, Arizona, Utah, and Oklahoma.

"The supply side will determine what housing or rent prices people will face in 18 to 24 months," study co-author Nicholas Irwin said. "And through political action, community members can encourage more development and put pressure on elected leaders to become accountable for rising housing prices."

New permits nationally fell in September—5.2% month over month and 7.4% year over year to an annualized 1.22 million units. Builders in some of these markets are relying on concessions to attract more buyers, but there's no question their confidence is shaken in such a difficult housing market.

For the first nine months of the year, overall new-home sales are 2.9% below where they were in 2025, Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner says.

Permits have been the "lone bright spot" in a lot of difficult data, Berner adds.

Housing affordability was top of mind in many swing states this year, and Democrats and Republicans both said they favor reforms that make it easier to build homes. State laws this year could lead to permitting of more homes, especially accessory dwelling units.

UNLV based its study on permits per resident. In total, cities issued 968,187 housing permits nationwide, or abut 2.83 per 1,000 residents. That's essentially flat from the same time in 2025, but it's a 4.1% drop from the same time in 2023.

South Carolina topped the study, permitting 6.07 units per 1,000 residents, a 5% increase from where it was one year ago. Idaho followed at 6.4 units per 1,000 residents, and North Carolina came in third at 5.77 units per 1,000 residents.

Those three states also top a recent Realtor.com report on top new-construction markets.

"These states combine fast-growing economies with favorable new-construction environments to bring homebuyers a larger share of new builds on the market," Berner says.

While Florida, Texas, and Arizona are still in the top 10 states by number of permits, they've slowed the pace of permitting. Rhode Island, New York, and Massachusetts are near the bottom on number of permits, but they've seen notable jumps in how many homes they permit.

Overall, 26 states and the District of Columbia permitted more homes compared to the same time in 2025. The other 24 states permitted less. The biggest drops came in Nevada, whose permit-to-resident ratio is down 29%, and Vermont and Connecticut, which both dropped 18%.

Nevada, which permitted 12,662 units in 2025 and 8,986 this year, joins North Dakota in permitting fewer homes than its projected household growth. That could spell trouble for affordability long-term.

About 64% of the permitted units are single-family, and 3.5% were 2- to 4-unit homes. The remaining 32% of homes are multifamily of 5 or more units.

Much of the housing data this year tells a story of a difficult market for homebuilders, with little relief in sight. This year, Mortgage Bankers Association Chief Economist Mike Fratantoni predicted mortgage rates would remain around 7.3% for the rest of the year and hover above 7% through 2027.

And National Association of Realtors® Chief Economist Lawrence Yun predicted the existing-home sales volume would rise just 4% from last year, having revised that downward this year.

Homebuilders are using incentives to entice buyers, and yet there are more existing homes on the market to compete with newly built ones. Berner explains that's true in the Midwest, often a center of affordability, where demand for homes is softer. Growing cost of land and labor is also making it harder for builders to compete for buyers.

But homebuilders still seeking permits for many units also says something. A permit doesn't mean a home starts construction immediately; it signals future intent.

"Builders are facing diminished buyer demand and high input costs, causing them to slow down when it comes to beginning and finishing projects. But permitting them has held relatively steady," Berner says. "We take this as a sign that builders expect conditions to turn around in the near future, and they want to be ready to capitalize when they do."

The UNLV study points to how affordability has worsened in many areas since 2018, and building new homes is key to improving it.

“Alleviating challenges related to the housing crisis really comes down to a city’s ability to actually build housing," Shawn McCoy, the report's other co-author said. "People need to be able to afford their home, but if they can’t find a home to rent or buy at all, there’s going to be a problem."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5624. Red Hat adds agentic AI operations, stronger security in OpenShift 5 and RHEL updates

Red Hat Inc. today announced a major update to its OpenShift Kubernetes-based application development platform that adds artificial intelligence-powered troubleshooting, stronger security controls and simplified upgrades as the company seeks to make its hybrid cloud infrastructure easier to manage.

The company also announced new versions of Red Hat Enterprise Linux with enhanced protection against software tampering, AI-assisted system administration and post-quantum cryptography.

The releases, unveiled at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America in Salt Lake City, reflect Red Hat’s continuing initiatives to embed AI into enterprise infrastructure management while strengthening security across increasingly distributed environments.

Red Hat OpenShift 5, the first major version upgrade in seven years, extends the platform’s ability to manage containers, virtual machines and AI workloads within a common environment. It also broadens the OpenShift Lightspeed generative AI assistant into an agent capable of investigating operational problems and recommending corrective actions.

“It’s infusing intelligence into the platform with agent-based troubleshooting through a simple interface with Lightspeed and natural language,” said Chris Wright, Red Hat’s chief technology officer and senior vice president of global engineering.

The updated Lightspeed interface allows administrators to generate visualizations of system performance using natural-language requests. For example, an administrator can ask for central processing unit utilization over the previous week, add memory consumption and overlay application errors. The resulting charts can be saved to dashboards that update continuously.

More significantly, OpenShift 5 introduces agentic troubleshooting that automatically investigates cluster events. When problems occur, the system can examine related information, reason through possible causes and propose remediation steps. Administrators retain control over whether the recommended actions are executed.

The platform also includes an AI-driven upgrade planner that examines application dependencies, Kubernetes application programming interfaces and optional operators to identify potential compatibility problems before updates begin.

“It is easy to upgrade Kubernetes,” said Mike Barrett, Red Hat’s vice president and general manager of hybrid cloud platforms. “What is difficult is navigating all the things you’re running on top of Kubernetes.”

Security enhancements include hardened multitenancy, more extensive network isolation, automated certificate management and post-quantum cryptography for control-plane communications. The capabilities are aimed in part at sovereign cloud providers and regulated organizations that must maintain strict separation between tenants and demonstrate compliance with security requirements.

OpenShift 5 also supports automated graphics processing unit resource allocation across AI inference and traditional enterprise workloads, potentially improving utilization of that expensive computing infrastructure.

Unlike previous major platform transitions, OpenShift 5 can be installed as an in-place update from OpenShift 4, avoiding the need to reinstall software or migrate workloads, Red Hat said. A revised lifecycle approach provides greater predictability for customers operating long-lived enterprise applications and virtualized infrastructure.

“We are no longer asking you to reinstall or migrate to use more of our product,” Barrett said. “This is a simple upgrade.”

The company is emphasizing virtualization as an increasingly important part of its business. Barrett said OpenShift Virtualization has grown to an $800 million business as customers seek alternatives to traditional virtualization platforms.

It said NASA’s laboratory migrated approximately 2,400 virtual machines to OpenShift Virtualization, while Gates Corp. moved more than 1,300 virtual machines and reported a 50% increase in available compute capacity.

The forthcoming Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.3 and 9.9 releases extend the company’s security strategy to the operating system.

A principal addition in RHEL 10.3 is support for sealed images, which use customer-controlled cryptographic keys to verify operating system integrity from the bootloader through the kernel and root file system. The technology is designed to prevent unauthorized modifications and block compromised software components from running.

Red Hat is also introducing a Model Context Protocol server that allows compatible AI assistants to investigate live Linux systems while maintaining access controls. Integration with Performance Co-Pilot, an open-source toolkit for monitoring, recording, analyzing, and controlling infrastructure, enables agents to examine historical performance information alongside current system conditions to identify the causes of operational problems.

A self-managed version of the RHEL command-line assistant, available in developer preview, lets organizations run AI inference locally. The capability is intended for disconnected, air-gapped and regulated environments where sending operational information outside the organization may be prohibited.

The releases also introduce post-quantum cryptography support for applications built using the Go programming language, including integration of the post-quantum Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism encryption algorithm with the language’s Transport Layer Security implementation. Additional enhancements include updated developer toolchains and support for newer processor architectures.

Red Hat separately announced Developer Hub 2.1, an update to its enterprise developer portal that gives AI coding agents governed access to organizational information, approved software components and standardized development workflows. Through MCP integration, agents can discover existing services, follow established development procedures and perform authorized actions using enterprise tooling.

The update also introduces expanded AI asset cataloging, a context-aware assistant and a longer support lifecycle, increasing the release support window from six to 10 months. Developer Hub 2.1 is generally available, as is OpenShift 5, while the new RHEL versions are expected in the coming weeks.

#5623. Inside the 10,000-Square-Foot Billionaires Row Condo That Was Just Relisted for $75 Million

A sprawling eight-bedroom condo tucked away in the One57 tower on Billionaires Row has returned to the market.

The estate, with spectacular views of Midtown Manhattan, first hit the market for $90 million in June 2025 and was discounted to $75 million in August 2026. It is holding firm at that price.

Built in 2013, the 10,000-square-foot home high atop the Park Hyatt New York has similarly soared to the top spot on the week’s most expensive homes list.

The home occupies an entire floor and has walls of windows framing views spanning Central Park, the Hudson River, and beyond.

Amenities in what the listing calls “one of the most sought after homes in the world” include a chef's kitchen with high-end appliances, dining and entertaining spaces, and a living room with home cinema capabilities.

The primary suite has three walk-in dressing rooms, a sitting area, and a marble-clad bathroom with a soaking tub, a separate rain shower, a sauna, a steam room, and a treatment room.

There's also a corner library facing the Hudson River, a study, a playroom, and separate quarters for guests and staff, including a kitchenette that's ideal for “well-accommodated live-in assistance.”

More spectacular mansions to make the week's most expensive homes list include boxing legend Sugar Ray Leonard's Pacific Palisades, CA, compound; an ocean-to-lake Polynesian-style retreat in Manalapan, FL; and a reimagined desert estate in Paradise Valley, AZ.

The Colony at White Pine Canyon: This ski-in/ski-out estate is currently under construction and offers a buyer the opportunity to add personal touches.

The seven-bedroom home will have a “timeless” 14,406-square-foot interior and direct ski access to Canyons Resort. Amenities will include a wellness retreat with an infrared sauna, steam room, hot tub, cold plunge, and fitness studio, plus a home theater, private office, and ski preparation area. Other highlights will include natural stone details, “distinctive” ceilings, smoked glass, radiant heat, oxygenation-ready systems, and seven fireplaces. The 5,804-square-foot heated outdoor living space is designed for year-round entertaining.

The 5.35-acre mountain retreat will also have a guest casita with a private garage.

Kelly Hamlin of Summit Sotheby's International Realty is the listing agent.

Ocean Reef estate: This five-bedroom waterfront mansion has 180-degree views of the Intracoastal Waterway and Card Sound Bay.

Built in 2012, the 11,694-square-foot estate also has 5,300 square feet of outdoor living space. Architectural details include “century-old” reclaimed wood floors, rich walnut millwork, and Venetian plaster walls. The chef’s kitchen has concrete countertops, antique reclaimed tin accents, and custom tile sinks. The separate prep kitchen has a reclaimed Chicago brick arched ceiling and a stained-glass pocket door that connects the two kitchens.

Other highlights include two primary suites with private water-facing terraces, a media room with a star-detail ceiling, a clubroom with a custom bar, a 2,000-bottle wine cellar, two wine coolers, dual laundry rooms, an elevator, and built-in safes.

An oval pool and spa, a lighted tennis court with a viewing pavilion, a putting green, and a two-story guesthouse adjacent to the pool are also on the property.

Billionaires Row: This eight-bedroom condo in Midtown Manhattan’s luxury One57 tower occupies an entire floor and has spectacular views of Central Park and the Hudson River.
